items.body:
## Start here: the four pieces of the circulation

Before thinking about cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), picture blood making a loop: **body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body**. The right ventricle (RV) moves blood through the low-pressure pulmonary circulation; the left ventricle (LV) moves it through the higher-pressure systemic circulation. The aortic and pulmonary valves are outlet valves; the mitral and tricuspid valves are inlet valves. A valve that is stenotic is difficult to open and obstructs forward flow; a regurgitant valve leaks backwards.

![The four heart chambers and their connections · Heart Foundation NZ](set13-c1-g1.png)

![Pulmonary circulation: blood flow between the heart and lungs · Heart Foundation NZ](set13-c1-g2.png)

**Three pressures, three different ideas.** Preload means how filled and stretched a ventricle is before it contracts; clinically we judge this imperfectly using chamber size, filling pressures and response to carefully assessed fluid. Afterload is the force opposing ejection: for the LV it relates to arterial pressure and vascular resistance; for the RV it relates chiefly to pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). Contractility is the ventricle's own ability to generate force, independent of its loading conditions. It is possible to have a low BP because the heart is empty, because it is weak, because it is obstructed, or because arteries are excessively dilated. Those are different diagnoses requiring different treatments.

**Follow oxygen, not just pressure.** Cardiac output (CO) = heart rate × stroke volume. Tissue oxygen delivery (DO₂) = blood flow × arterial oxygen content. A good MAP does not guarantee good tissue oxygenation when flow or haemoglobin is low. Blood pressure is a consequence of flow and resistance, not a direct measure of oxygen delivery. This principle will make the bypass and difficult-weaning chapters understandable.

## The first abbreviations to know

**CABG** = coronary artery bypass grafting; **AVR/MVR** = aortic/mitral valve replacement; **CPB** = cardiopulmonary bypass; **TOE** (TEE in American texts) = transoesophageal echocardiography, the ultrasound probe in the oesophagus used to inspect the heart during surgery; **TTE** = transthoracic echocardiography, imaging through the chest. **MAP** = mean arterial pressure; **SVR** = systemic vascular resistance; **PVR** = pulmonary vascular resistance; **PAP** = pulmonary artery pressure; **CVP** = central venous pressure; **RWMA** = regional wall-motion abnormality (a heart segment moving poorly); **LVOT/RVOT** = left/right ventricular outflow tract. Each subsequent chapter explains technical terms when they first become clinically important.

**What the team members do.** The surgeon operates on coronary vessels, valves or aorta. The perfusionist operates the bypass machine and monitors circuit blood flow, oxygenator gases, anticoagulation and temperature in coordination with the team. The anaesthetist manages anaesthesia, the airway, haemodynamics, anticoagulation checks, blood products, monitoring and the return to the patient's own circulation. Safe cardiac anaesthesia depends on explicit communication between all three.

## Why cardiac surgery is a distinct anaesthetic problem

In most anaesthetics the circulation continues to deliver oxygen while surgery changes the patient’s physiology. In conventional on-pump cardiac surgery we deliberately stop, isolate or manipulate the heart, and transfer oxygen delivery to an extracorporeal circuit. The anaesthetist’s challenge is therefore not only to maintain haemodynamic stability: it is to hand the circulation safely to the bypass machine and later take it back. A patient with good haemodynamics before CPB may return with myocardial stunning, air, valve dysfunction, residual ischaemia, vasoplegia or coagulopathy. Successful separation is a diagnosis and a coordinated transition, not simply reducing pump flow.

The simplest mental model is **four phases**:

- **1.** **Before bypass:** assess reserve, induce and monitor safely, prepare for bleeding, pacing and circulatory collapse.
- **2.** **On bypass:** maintain cerebral/systemic oxygen delivery and anaesthesia while the perfusionist controls flow, oxygenation, gas exchange and temperature; the surgeon protects and repairs the heart.
- **3.** **Separating from bypass:** warm, ventilate and fill the heart, restore rhythm and contractility, interrogate the repair, de-air, then progressively transfer flow back to the native circulation.
- **4.** **After bypass and in ICU:** reverse anticoagulation, secure haemostasis, distinguish surgical bleeding from acquired coagulopathy and detect low cardiac output, tamponade, neurological injury and other early complications.

## A typical uncomplicated on-pump cardiac operation

| Stage                           | What happens                                                                                | Why the anaesthetist cares                                                                                                         |
|---------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Induction and monitoring        | Arterial line, appropriate venous access, GA, TOE/TEE where indicated, antibiotics          | Coronary/valve disease makes hypotension, tachycardia and loss of rhythm dangerous. Establish baseline ventricular/valve findings. |
| Sternotomy and dissection       | Median sternotomy, pericardial opening, conduit harvest when relevant                       | Bleeding, ischaemia, haemodynamic effects of manipulation; redo cases can injure heart before bypass is available.                 |
| Anticoagulation and cannulation | Systemic heparin, confirm adequate ACT, venous drainage and arterial return cannulae        | Inadequate anticoagulation can clot the circuit. Aortic atheroma changes safe cannulation strategy.                                |
| Initiate CPB                    | Venous blood drains, pump sends it through oxygenator and heat exchanger to arterial system | Check systemic flow, arterial pressure, venous return, gas exchange and adequate depth of anaesthesia.                             |
| Clamp and cardioplegia          | Aortic cross-clamp isolates coronary circulation, cardioplegia arrests/protects myocardium  | Cardioplegia delivery and myocardial protection determine the ability to separate later.                                           |
| Surgical repair                 | CABG distal/proximal anastomoses or valve replacement/repair                                | Need de-airing, venting and communication about lesions and residual pathology.                                                    |
| Reperfusion and separation      | Cross-clamp removed, rewarming, ventilation/rhythm restored, flow returned to patient       | This is when ventricular dysfunction, LVOT obstruction, RV failure and vasoplegia become visible.                                  |
| Protamine and haemostasis       | Heparin reversed, decannulation, drain placement, closure                                   | Protamine reactions, residual heparin, fibrinolysis, platelet dysfunction and surgical bleeding.                                   |
| Intensive care                  | Haemodynamic/ventilatory handover, warming, analgesia, extubation when safe                 | Early complication surveillance and goal-directed organ support.                                                                   |

items.body:
## How to make sense of an echocardiogram before cardiac surgery

You do not need to be a cardiac echocardiographer to understand the preoperative report. Read it in this order:

- **1.** **What is the main lesion?** Coronary ischaemia, valve obstruction/leak, or an aortic problem?
- **2.** **How is the LV pumping?** Ejection fraction (EF) measures the fraction of LV end-diastolic volume ejected each beat, not necessarily forward flow: severe mitral regurgitation can have a reassuring-looking EF because blood exits backwards into the left atrium.
- **3.** **What is the RV like?** It may be the limiting chamber after bypass even when LV EF is normal.
- **4.** **Are there high filling pressures or pulmonary hypertension?** A stiff LV may have adequate EF but high left atrial pressure and pulmonary oedema risk.
- **5.** **Are there other valves, shunts, aortic atheroma or pericardial effusion?**

A **regional wall-motion abnormality (RWMA)** means one coronary-supplied part of the LV contracts poorly compared with its neighbours. It may reflect previous infarction or new ischaemia. After CABG, a new RWMA is a warning that the corresponding graft or coronary territory needs assessment. **TOE** provides real-time intraoperative imaging; it can show an empty small ventricle (possible insufficient filling), a distended poorly contracting chamber (failure), mitral regurgitation, residual valve obstruction and intracardiac air. TOE must be interpreted together with pressure, flow, rhythm and surgery—not as a single definitive number.

![Mid-oesophageal four-chamber TOE view · Brazilian perioperative TOE consensus](set13-c2-g1.png)

![Mid-oesophageal long-axis TOE view · Brazilian perioperative TOE consensus](set13-c2-g2.png)

![Transgastric mid-papillary short-axis TOE view · Brazilian perioperative TOE consensus](set13-c2-g3.png)

## How the Heart Team decides between a catheter procedure and an operation

A coronary narrowing may be treated with medical therapy, a stent (PCI), or CABG; a diseased aortic valve may be treated with surgery or TAVI. There is no universal answer from the ECG or echo alone. The **Heart Team** considers the anatomical complexity, expected durability, LV and RV function, surgical frailty, coronary disease, antithrombotic requirements and the patient’s goals. As an anaesthetist, you should be able to explain **why this patient is having this operation rather than a catheter intervention** and what physiological risk this choice introduces. For example, extensive coronary disease may favour bypass surgery, whereas a suitable high-risk patient with severe AS may be offered transfemoral TAVI.

Cardiac surgical scores such as **EuroSCORE II** and **STS** estimate population-based operative risk; they do not replace examination of the actual coronary/valve anatomy or the likely hazards of anaesthetic induction, aortic cannulation, CPB and postoperative organ dysfunction. Separately ask if the operation is elective, urgent or rescue after failed PCI, because the antiplatelet exposure, bleeding risk and likelihood of cardiogenic shock differ.

Coronary angiography: identify the left main bifurcation into LAD and circumflex, the RCA and whether the posterior descending artery arises from RCA or circumflex (dominance). Relate threatened territories to operative graft targets. For echo, assess regional wall motion, LV and RV size/function, valve gradients and regurgitation, pulmonary pressure estimate and pericardial space. Compare reports with symptoms, ECG and haemodynamics; a normal EF does not exclude ischaemia, diastolic dysfunction or RV failure. A new major clinical change warrants reassessment rather than automatically relying on an old echo.

## Preoperative assessment: find what may prevent safe induction or separation

History and examination should establish symptoms, **functional reserve, coronary anatomy, ventricular and valve function, pulmonary vascular/right-ventricular status, cerebrovascular and renal disease**, frailty and bleeding risk. Review the operation and the reason for it: unstable angina needing CABG has different immediate risk from chronic severe AS requiring AVR. Ask about previous sternotomy, PCI, antiplatelets, anticoagulants, infection/endocarditis, pulmonary disease and previous problems with airway, bleeding or anaesthesia.

| Information                                                     | Why it changes the plan                                                                                                                                        |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Coronary angiography / CT                                       | Left-main or proximal LAD disease, right-dominant circulation, graft targets, residual stenoses and potentially jeopardised territories.                       |
| TTE/TOE                                                         | LV/RV systolic function, diastolic filling, valve severity, pulmonary pressure, effusion, shunt and aortic disease. Note baseline lesions before starting CPB. |
| ECG / rhythm / device                                           | Recent ischaemia, conduction disease, AF, paced rhythm and the need for pacing/defibrillation.                                                                 |
| FBC, creatinine/electrolytes, LFT/coagulation, group and screen | Anaemia, renal vulnerability, electrolyte-mediated arrhythmia, transfusion preparation and anticoagulation issues.                                             |
| Carotid/aortic imaging when indicated                           | Prior stroke, carotid disease or heavily diseased aorta changes cerebral protection/cannulation. Screening is selective, not automatic.                        |
| Risk models: EuroSCORE II / STS                                 | Support informed risk discussion but cannot replace lesion-specific physiological judgement.                                                                   |

**Red flags requiring optimisation or a different plan:** decompensated HF, recent ACS, rapid arrhythmia, active infection, critical anaemia, severe pulmonary hypertension/RV dysfunction, or a severely calcified ascending aorta. When time allows, address preoperative anaemia and iron deficiency, nutrition, smoking, diabetes and renal risk. Balance cessation of P2Y12 inhibitors against ACS/stent and urgent-surgery risk using a cardiology–surgical decision; use contemporary cardiac-surgery medication guidance rather than transplanting non-cardiac surgery rules.

## Anxiety and premedication (SS_CS 1.3)

Cardiac patients may be frightened of sternotomy, CPB, postoperative ventilation, mortality or ICU care. Anxiety increases sympathetic drive, myocardial oxygen demand and blood pressure. **First-line treatment is information and reassurance:** explain the sequence, monitoring, analgesia, expectation of drains and ventilation, and the postoperative destination; invite specific questions and address misconceptions. Quiet surroundings, a familiar support person when possible, language/cultural support and psychological strategies can outperform reflex sedation.

When pharmacological anxiolysis is appropriate, individualise a small oral/IV benzodiazepine dose or a short-acting titrated alternative according to age, frailty, airway/OSA, respiratory reserve, hepatic impairment and haemodynamics. An illustrative monitored option is midazolam 0.5–1 mg IV titrated, rather than a fixed standard dose; consider avoiding in older/frail patients at risk of delirium. Dexmedetomidine can provide anxiolysis/sympatholysis but may produce bradycardia/hypotension and is not a universal premedication. In unstable coronary disease or critical AS, even modest sedation can reduce respiratory drive or systemic pressure. Continue necessary anti-anginal therapy and plan analgesia and reassurance as part of a coherent strategy.

## Before induction: practical preparation

- **Team briefing:** surgeon, perfusionist and anaesthetist agree on cannulation, CPB plan, cardioplegia, temperature, major anticipated difficulties, rescue bypass/MCS and transfusion.
- **Monitoring:** standard ANZCA monitoring, ECG ST analysis, invasive arterial pressure (consider before induction), large-bore IVs, central venous access when appropriate, temperature at more than one site during CPB, urine output, TOF, arterial/venous blood gases and haemoglobin. TOE is valuable for baseline ventricular/valve assessment and later de-airing/repair. Cerebral NIRS/processed EEG as appropriate.
- **Rescue readiness:** blood and rapid infuser, cardioversion/defibrillation, pacing, vasoactive infusions, difficult airway equipment, availability of bypass for high-risk induction.
- **Induction:** choose smooth and titrated drugs rather than a rigid recipe. Propofol may markedly reduce SVR; etomidate causes relatively little immediate haemodynamic depression but has disadvantages; ketamine may increase demand and can depress catecholamine-depleted hearts. Opioid-based balanced anaesthesia and early vasopressor are common. Select goals from the underlying lesion (CAD: avoid tachycardia/ischaemia; AS: preserve coronary perfusion; MR: avoid excessive afterload; severe RV failure: avoid PVR rise).

## Re-do cardiac surgery: why the first incision can be the most dangerous (SS_CS 1.15)

A repeat operation is not just "the same operation again". Registry data put 30-day mortality at roughly two to six times the rate for a first operation. Most of the direct risk comes from scar tissue under the sternum, but it also reflects longer operations, more bleeding and sicker patients. Experienced centres with good imaging and a rehearsed rescue plan report much smaller excess risk, so the aim is to predict the hazard and plan for it.

### Technical and anatomical problems

- **Adhesions and scar:** the right ventricle, right atrium, ascending aorta, grafts and lungs can be bound to the back of the sternum like glue. Most of the direct risk of redo surgery comes from these adhesions.
- **Re-entry injury:** the saw or the first dissection can lacerate the right ventricle, aorta, innominate vein or a patent graft stuck to the bone. In a series of 2,555 cardiac reoperations, 9.0% of patients had an injury. Hospital mortality was 18.5% with injury and 6.5% without, and 25% when the injury happened during sternal division.
- **Who is injured:** injury was more common after previous CABG (11% vs 7%), and when the current operation was aortic surgery (14% vs 8%) or aortic valve replacement (10% vs 8%).
- **Not only at sternotomy:** in a Cleveland Clinic review of 1,847 reoperations, 7% had an intraoperative adverse event, most often during dissection before bypass was started. Typical events were injury to grafts, cardiac chambers or great vessels, life-threatening arrhythmia, and lung injury severe enough to change the operation. Death, stroke or MI occurred in 19% with an event and 6.2% without.
- **Grafts at risk:** a patent internal mammary graft must be found and protected, because clamping or injuring it can infarct a large territory. In a redo mitral series, injury to a patent LIMA graft independently predicted death (odds ratio 4.2), and a major cardiovascular injury at re-entry was a much stronger predictor (odds ratio 19.2).
- **Longer operations:** dissecting scar lengthens the operation and the bypass run. In the same series, each extra increment of bypass time independently predicted death.

### Physiological and clinical consequences

- **Bleeding and transfusion:** large raw dissected surfaces, a longer pump run, heparin and coagulopathy all add up. In 6,021 resternotomies at one centre, 66% to 77% of patients received blood products (the highest rate was in redo within a year). In the redo mitral series, 28.0% had a massive transfusion, 7.6% returned to theatre for bleeding, and transfusion of more than six units independently predicted death (odds ratio 4.4).
- **Organ dysfunction:** in that mitral series, acute renal insufficiency occurred in 16.1%, respiratory insufficiency in 14.8%, stroke in 4.9%, MI in 5.9% and a new permanent pacemaker in 10.1%. Needing a ventilator for more than 48 hours increased the odds of death about five-fold. These figures come from redo mitral surgery specifically, so use them as examples of the pattern and not as figures for every redo operation.
- **Hard to rescue:** if a major injury happens before bypass is running, the patient can lose circulation within minutes, which is why access and bypass are planned before the saw is used.

### Patient factors

- **Older and sicker:** patients needing a second operation are usually older, with progressed vascular disease and worse heart and kidney function than at the first operation.
- **Predictors of death after redo surgery** in the Cleveland Clinic series: non-elective surgery, lower haematocrit, higher creatinine, higher NYHA class and lower ejection fraction.
- **Number of previous operations and chest radiotherapy** both raise the risk of injury at re-entry. Severe right heart failure makes the situation less forgiving.
- **Interval since the last operation:** across 6,021 resternotomies operative mortality was about 3% to 4% whatever the interval, so a long gap is not automatically safer. Early redo (under one year) had more transfusion and longer operations, and isolated redo CABG within a year looked worse in a small number of patients, so treat that last finding with caution.

### What the anaesthetist does

**Preoperative:** obtain previous operation notes and graft maps. A CT scan shows how close the sternum is to the heart, aorta and grafts, and angiography confirms which grafts are patent. Identify anticoagulants and redo-associated bleeding risk. Match the rescue plan to the imaging-predicted risk, from lowest to highest:
- **1.** Perfusionist in the room with the circuit primed
- **2.** Axillary or femoral vessels exposed
- **3.** Bypass established through peripheral cannulation **before** the sternum is opened
- **4.** Hypothermic circulatory arrest for the very highest-risk anatomy

Starting bypass early is not free: it lengthens the pump run and increases coagulopathic bleeding and organ dysfunction, so it is reserved for the highest-risk patients. Peripheral cannulation can itself cause bleeding, dissection or limb ischaemia. Agree the plan at a team huddle.

**Intraoperative:** large-bore access and blood immediately available, invasive pressure and skilled TOE, with the surgeon and perfusionist present for induction and re-entry. Defibrillator pads go on before induction. Surgeons commonly use an oscillating saw, may leave the sternal wires in to protect adherent structures, and avoid touching patent vein grafts. Plan cardioplegia around a patent mammary graft; combined antegrade and retrograde delivery was associated with lower mortality in the redo mitral series. If major injury occurs, communicate immediately, compress or control the bleeding, replace volume with blood, rapidly establish CPB using the pre-agreed access and treat myocardial ischaemia.

**Postoperative:** expect more bleeding, transfusion, prolonged CPB, RV dysfunction and a longer ICU stay. Watch for return to theatre for bleeding, acute kidney injury, prolonged ventilation, stroke and conduction block needing pacing.

![CT views of a bypass graft and the RV immediately behind the sternum · BJA Education 2024](set13-c2-g4.png)

items.title: 3. Coronary bypass and valve surgery
items.body:
## Coronary anatomy and valve pathology

![Coronary arteries and their branches · Lynch/Häggström, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0](set13-c3-cor.png)

### Coronary arteries: the heart's own blood supply

- The myocardium is supplied by coronary arteries that branch off the aortic root.
- The **left main** artery divides into the LAD and the circumflex.
- **LAD** (left anterior descending artery):
  - Runs down the front of the heart.
  - Supplies much of the anterior LV wall and the septum.
  - Its diagonal branches supply the anterolateral wall.
- **Circumflex:**
  - Runs in the groove between the left atrium and LV.
  - Supplies much of the lateral LV wall through its oblique marginal branches.
- **RCA** (right coronary artery):
  - Supplies the right ventricle (acute marginal branch) and often the inferior LV wall (posterior descending artery).
  - Often supplies the SA and AV nodes, so RCA ischaemia can cause bradycardia or heart block.
- **Dominance** is defined by which artery gives off the posterior descending artery (PDA) at the back of the heart (the crux), and so supplies the inferior wall and posterior septum:
  - **Right dominant (about 70%):** the RCA gives the PDA. The RCA supplies the RV, the inferior wall and the posterior septum.
  - **Left dominant (about 10–15%):** the circumflex gives the PDA. The RCA is small and supplies mainly the RV, and the circumflex supplies the lateral and inferior walls.
  - **Co-dominant (the remainder):** both arteries contribute to the PDA.
  - The dominant artery usually supplies the AV node, so an occlusion of it is more likely to cause heart block. This is why the diagram's territories differ between patients.
- A fixed stenosis limits flow, especially when the heart needs more oxygen.
- CABG does not remove the plaque. It builds a new conduit to supply myocardium beyond the narrowing.
- A **LIMA–LAD** graft takes the left internal mammary artery and connects it to the LAD.
- A vein graft connects a segment of saphenous vein between the aorta and a coronary artery beyond the narrowing.

![Myocardial territories supplied by each coronary artery · TeachMeAnatomy](set13-c3-terr2.png)

### Valves: each lesion causes a different problem

- **Aortic stenosis (AS):**
  - The LV must generate a very high pressure to eject through a tight outlet.
  - The LV becomes thick and stiff.
- **Aortic regurgitation (AR):**
  - Aortic blood leaks back into the LV during diastole.
  - The LV carries an increased volume load.
- **Mitral stenosis (MS):**
  - Blood cannot empty easily from the left atrium to the LV.
  - Pulmonary venous pressure rises.
- **Mitral regurgitation (MR):**
  - Blood leaves the LV both forwards into the aorta and backwards into the left atrium during systole.
- These mechanisms explain why one generic haemodynamic plan will not work for CABG, AVR and mitral surgery.

### Surgical words you will keep seeing

- **Anastomosis:** the connection between two vessels or structures.
- **Sternotomy:** the sternum is divided to access the heart.
- **Cross-clamp:** blocks aortic flow between the pump return and the heart, creating a still operative field.
- **De-airing:** removes gas from the heart and aortic root before blood is pumped to the brain and coronary arteries.

Recognise the LM, LAD, LCx and RCA. Relate new regional ischaemia on ECG or TOE to the coronary territory.

## Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)

CABG creates a conduit beyond a stenotic epicardial coronary artery. Common grafts are **LIMA→LAD**, radial artery and saphenous vein. The LIMA generally has excellent long-term patency; radial grafts may be prone to spasm, whereas vein grafts have greater long-term atherosclerotic failure. The surgeon selects targets based on anatomy, run-off and viability; a patent graft is no guarantee of adequate perfusion if distal disease is severe.

![Coronary bypass conduits route blood around obstructed native vessels · NHLBI](set13-c3-g2.png)

**On-pump CABG steps:** sternotomy/conduit harvest → systemic heparinisation → aortic and venous cannulation → CPB → cross-clamp/cardioplegia → distal graft anastomoses on arrested myocardium → proximal anastomoses to ascending aorta when required (or composite graft strategy) → de-airing/reperfusion → wean/protamine/haemostasis/closure. A side-biting clamp for proximal grafts can itself embolise aortic plaque; anaortic techniques can reduce manipulation in selected patients.

**Off-pump CABG (OPCAB):** following heparinisation, a mechanical stabiliser immobilises a small epicardial area while the heart continues beating. The surgeon positions/displaces the heart to access target vessels; an intracoronary shunt may maintain distal flow during the anastomosis. A standby pump/perfusionist and clear conversion trigger are essential.

**Anaesthetic physiology:** heart displacement reduces venous return, impairs RV filling and worsens MR or regional ischaemia; loss of output is often greatest when exposing posterior/lateral targets. Use careful preload, position adjustments, judicious vasopressor/inotrope and TOE; communicate before destabilising manipulation. Rescue severe ischaemia by releasing displacement, restoring perfusion and converting to CPB when necessary. Avoid inappropriate large fluid loading just to maintain BP.

**On versus off pump:** avoiding CPB can reduce circuit-related exposure. Aortic manipulation depends on the surgical technique. CORONARY found similar five-year major outcomes. ROOBY showed worse five-year survival with off-pump surgery in its largely male veteran population. Consider aortic disease, completeness of revascularisation and surgical expertise.

## CABG: perioperative anaesthetic management

**The operation only makes sense if you know which myocardium is at risk.** Every decision below follows from the angiogram, the ventricle and the phase of surgery.

### Preoperative

**Look at the angiogram, not the label "three-vessel disease":**

- Left-main disease, critical proximal LAD stenosis and severe lesions supplying collateral-dependent myocardium mean that even a brief fall in diastolic pressure may cause widespread ischaemia.
- Document previous infarct territories, LV ejection fraction and regional function. A normal global EF can coexist with an important threatened territory.
- Ask about angina at rest, pulmonary oedema or escalating anti-anginal therapy, because these change the urgency and suitability of a leisurely elective preparation.
- Define LV/RV dysfunction, aortic atheroma and ability to tolerate induction.

**Medications and risk review:**

- **Review:** aspirin and P2Y12 history (ACS, recent stent, urgency, bleeding risk), haemoglobin and iron status, renal function, diabetes including SGLT2 inhibitors, carotid/cerebrovascular symptoms and aortic atheroma.
- **Aspirin:** generally continued for isolated CABG unless there is a specific reason not to.
- **P2Y12 washout (when elective surgery allows):** the 2024 EACTS medication guideline suggests at least **3 days for ticagrelor, 5 for clopidogrel and 7 for prasugrel**.
  - These are cardiac-surgical bleeding-oriented intervals.
  - They are not permission to interrupt recent-stent therapy without cardiology input.
- **ACS:** an earlier operation may be safer than withholding revascularisation. A platelet-function assay may help estimate residual drug effect where available.
- **Beta-blocker and statin:** continue when appropriate.
- **RAAS inhibitors and diuretics:** individualise to ventricular function and haemodynamics.
- **Goal:** not simply a normal BP, but adequate coronary perfusion pressure in every phase of surgery.
- Continue chronic anti-anginal therapy and agree the antithrombotic plan.

[EACTS perioperative medication guideline](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae355)

### Intraoperative

**Induction: why it is hazardous**

- Hypnosis removes sympathetic compensation and commonly reduces SVR. Intubation creates a short catecholamine surge.
- Both directions can harm: a fall in aortic diastolic pressure reduces flow beyond a fixed stenosis, whereas tachycardia shortens diastole and raises oxygen consumption.
- Prepare arterial-pressure monitoring and vasopressors **before** induction, and titrate opioid and hypnotic doses to the patient.
- Treat a new ST change together with BP and TOE findings.
- A single absolute heart-rate target is less useful than preserving the patient's known tolerated rate while avoiding abrupt tachycardia and bradycardia with low output.
- Use ECG and TOE for regional function throughout.

**Before cross-clamping**

- Mammary-artery harvest, manipulation of the heart and sternotomy can change loading and provoke ischaemia.
- Agree before the aortic cannula or cross-clamp goes on whether the ascending aorta is suitable for instrumentation. Epiaortic ultrasound can be more sensitive than palpation for dangerous plaque.
- If a radial artery will be used as a graft, agree an alternative arterial line site (usually the contralateral side).
- Record a baseline TOE of LV/RV function, valve pathology, regional wall motion and aortic findings, so that changes after reperfusion are recognised as new.
- Heparinise before cannulation and ensure anaesthesia on bypass.

**After grafting: interpret the TOE in the light of the anatomy**

- **New anteroseptal RWMA after LIMA–LAD grafting:** suggests inadequate LAD perfusion, air, graft kinking/spasm or anastomotic failure. Restore perfusion and inspect the graft, not merely increase adrenaline.
- **Inferior dysfunction:** may indicate RCA/PDA territory ischaemia or an RV problem.
- Reperfusion arrhythmias, graft spasm, bleeding and temperature or electrolyte disturbances can coexist.
- Effective de-airing and graded separation are essential.
- Until evaluated, treat any new regional wall-motion abnormality as graft-related ischaemia or air.

### Postoperative

- Surveillance for bleeding, myocardial injury, arrhythmia, low output and respiratory dysfunction.
- Distinguish expected post-cardiac-surgery troponin elevation from graft-related MI using clinical deterioration, ECG, serial values, echo and sometimes emergency angiography.
- Restart antiplatelet therapy safely.

Postoperatively: continue close ECG, haemodynamics and graft-territory surveillance; restart aspirin early when haemostasis permits (cardiac medication guideline generally within 24 h, ideally within 6 h after CABG), and plan P2Y12 resumption if ACS/recent PCI requires it. Maintain statin and beta-blocker therapy as tolerated. Assess new ST elevation, low output or arrhythmia urgently with ECG/echo and cardiology/surgeon input; investigate a mechanical graft problem rather than treating troponin alone.

## Off-pump CABG: follow the haemodynamics as the heart is moved

Off-pump surgery is not simply "CABG without the pump". The surgeon needs a nearly motionless target, achieved with a stabiliser, while the rest of the heart beats in an abnormal position. The key anaesthetic skill is anticipating **which position impairs which cardiac chamber**.

| Surgical moment                       | Typical physiological problem                                                       | First response and rationale                                                                                                                                        |
|---------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Anterior LAD anastomosis              | Local coronary occlusion and ischaemia, generally less displacement                 | Control HR/BP, watch ST and regional function; intracoronary shunt if needed.                                                                                       |
| Lateral wall / obtuse marginal target | Verticalisation/compression reduces RV inflow, twists the heart and may increase MR | Ask surgeon to reduce displacement immediately if output falls; inspect with TOE, restore perfusion pressure, use small fluid increments only if truly underfilled. |
| Inferior/posterior target             | Marked heart elevation may obstruct venous return/RVOT and trigger arrhythmia       | Optimise positioning and stabiliser, maintain preload and coronary perfusion, use vasoactive support as a bridge to completing the anastomosis.                     |
| Intracoronary snare/anastomosis       | Brief regional ischaemia and electrical instability                                 | Monitor ST/RWMA; release occlusion or use shunt if unsafe; maintain readiness for urgent CPB conversion.                                                            |

### If pressure or output falls during displacement

- **Think mechanical first:** a low arterial pressure during displacement usually reflects **mechanical impediment to filling or ejection** (impaired RV filling, distorted atrioventricular inflow, compression from the stabiliser), not primary contractile failure.
- **Compare with the position before displacement:** arterial pulsatility, CVP, ST segments and TOE.
- **Tell the surgeon promptly** if there is loss of waveform or pulsatility, severe ST change, VT/VF or sustained low output.
- **Ask the surgeon to release displacement and stabiliser pressure.** This is often the fastest effective treatment.
- **Support perfusion:** test small, reassessed preload changes and use a titrated vasopressor to maintain coronary perfusion pressure if needed.
- **Avoid large fluid volumes.** They are inappropriate for a mechanical problem and can distend the RV and impair exposure.

### When to convert to CPB

Agree the threshold with the team **before** stabilisation. Convert promptly, rather than tolerate prolonged compromised perfusion, if there is:

- persistent regional ischaemia despite manoeuvres
- sustained or refractory arrhythmia
- falling cardiac index despite repositioning
- failure to obtain a safe anastomotic field, or inability to expose targets safely
- incomplete revascularisation

### Graft selection and aortic manipulation

- **Internal thoracic artery:** commonly supplies the LAD.
- **Radial graft:** needs suitable hand collateral circulation and a sufficiently stenosed target to limit competitive flow. Check the intended harvest site before choosing arterial access.
- **Ascending aortic calcification:** changes cannulation, clamp and graft plans. Epiaortic ultrasound can help locate a safe site or show that another strategy is needed.
- **Side-biting clamp:** off-pump surgery can still use one for a proximal anastomosis.
- **Anaortic strategy:** avoids aortic manipulation, typically using in situ or composite grafts where suitable. It can help in a heavily atheromatous aorta.

### What the trials show

- CORONARY found similar five-year major outcomes with off-pump and on-pump surgery. ROOBY showed worse five-year survival with off-pump surgery in its largely male veteran population.
- Neither supports declaring off-pump universally better. Benefit depends on surgeon expertise, patient anatomy and completeness of grafting.

[BJA Education CABG Part 1, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.08.003) · [Adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/)

![Aortic stenosis with mitral regurgitation (left) and aortic regurgitation (right) · Cleveland Clinic](set13-c3-valves.jpg)

## Valve lesion haemodynamic goals

| **Lesion** | **Preload and rhythm**                                                      | **Afterload and contractility**                                                         |
|------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| AS         | Adequate preload, sinus rhythm, avoid marked tachy/bradycardia              | Maintain diastolic pressure and SVR, avoid abrupt vasodilation; maintain contractility. |
| AR         | Avoid bradycardia; maintain forward volume without overload                 | Avoid acute increases in SVR; maintain forward output and coronary pressure.            |
| MS         | Controlled rate, preserve sinus rhythm if feasible; avoid overfilling LA/RV | Maintain systemic pressure, prevent PVR rise; cautiously titrate contractility support. |
| MR         | Maintain forward flow; avoid bradycardia and marked congestion              | Avoid excessive SVR; anticipate LV afterload mismatch after repair.                     |

**Why each lesion needs a different approach:**

- **AS:**
  - The LV needs a high pressure to push blood through the narrowed valve.
  - A sudden fall in aortic diastolic pressure cuts coronary perfusion while the thick LV needs more oxygen.
  - Tachycardia shortens coronary filling time.
- **AR:**
  - Blood runs back from the aorta into the LV during diastole.
  - A longer diastole (bradycardia) gives more time for regurgitation.
- **MS:**
  - The narrowed mitral opening slows LV filling and keeps pulmonary venous pressure high.
  - Tachycardia shortens diastole and worsens pulmonary congestion.
- **MR:**
  - The LV ejects partly into the lower-pressure left atrium, so the EF looks deceptively reassuring.
  - After repair or replacement the leak is gone, so the LV works against higher effective resistance.
- These are starting tendencies, not rules. Coexisting coronary disease, ventricular failure or pulmonary hypertension can change the plan.

### Why arrhythmia and conduction block are common with AVR

**Conduction block (AV block, bundle branch block)**

- The AV node and His bundle run in the septum just beneath the aortic annulus, close to the junction of the right and non-coronary cusps.
- Debriding calcium from the annulus, placing sutures and seating the prosthesis all happen next to this tissue. Direct injury, a suture through the conduction tissue, or oedema and haematoma from surgical trauma can block conduction.
- Calcific stenosis often extends into the septum, so more debridement is needed and the conduction tissue is already stressed.
- An oversized prosthesis or a deep, tight annular fit can press on the conduction tissue.
- Block may appear at weaning from bypass or develop over the following days. Many cases settle as the swelling resolves, but persistent complete block needs a permanent pacemaker. This is why pacing wires are placed and pacing must be ready.
- Pre-existing conduction disease (for example first-degree AV block or bundle branch block) increases the risk.

**Ventricular arrhythmia**

- A hypertrophied LV with high LVEDP and limited coronary reserve is vulnerable to subendocardial ischaemia, and cardioplegia may be distributed unevenly through it.
- Ischaemia–reperfusion after cross-clamp release, together with potassium and magnesium shifts, makes VF or VT common at unclamping.

**Atrial fibrillation and atrial arrhythmia**

- The atria are stretched by long-standing valve disease and a high-pressure LV, and are often enlarged.
- Surgery adds atrial ischaemia (inadequate atrial protection during arrest), cannulation and manipulation, surgical inflammation, high sympathetic drive, pain, and electrolyte or volume shifts.
- Postoperative AF typically appears in the first few days. It is poorly tolerated by a stiff, hypertrophied LV that depends on atrial contraction for filling, so it can cause sudden haemodynamic collapse.

**What this means in practice**

- **Intraop:** correct potassium and magnesium, have defibrillation and pacing ready for unclamping and separation, and watch for new AV block.
- **Postop:** monitor rhythm and conduction continuously, keep electrolytes in range, treat pain, and treat AF promptly.

## Aortic valve replacement (AVR)

**Before surgery, distinguish AS from AR.** These are different anaesthetic problems even though both require AVR.

- **Severe AS:**
  - Small, thick, stiff LV with high filling pressure and a narrow coronary perfusion reserve.
  - Induction hypotension and loss of atrial contraction can cause collapse.
  - On echo, typical high-gradient severe AS has peak velocity ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mmHg and valve area ≤1.0 cm².
  - Low-flow/low-gradient severe disease may meet fewer criteria and needs further evaluation.
- **Chronic severe AR:**
  - LV volume loading, often low diastolic aortic pressure and a large compliant ventricle.
  - Excessive bradycardia lengthens diastole and can increase regurgitation.
  - Chronic dilatation masks declining reserve.
- **Acute AR:**
  - Acute regurgitation into a non-compliant LV rapidly raises LVEDP.
  - It can cause shock and fulminant pulmonary oedema, because the LV has had no time to remodel.

Choose induction and haemodynamic rescue according to the lesion and the reserve, rather than a fixed heart-rate target.

### Surgical sequence

- **1.** Sternotomy, systemic heparinisation and cannulation.
- **2.** Establish CPB.
- **3.** Cross-clamp and give cardioplegia.
- **4.** Open the aorta, remove the diseased valve and implant a mechanical or tissue prosthesis.
- **5.** Close the aorta, de-air, unclamp, reperfuse and assess with TOE.

### Implications

- In severe AR, antegrade root cardioplegia may leak into and distend the LV. Selective coronary ostial or retrograde coronary-sinus delivery may be required.
- Root or annular enlargement, if necessary, increases operative and myocardial ischaemic time.
- Calcium or tissue debris can embolise.
- Injury to the nearby conduction system may cause complete heart block, so pacing must be ready.

### After implantation

**The loading conditions have changed.**

- Relieving AS suddenly lowers LV afterload, but the hypertrophied myocardium may still be stiff and ischaemia-prone.
- Correcting AR removes diastolic volume overload and may unmask underlying LV impairment.

**If the patient cannot separate from bypass, check:**

- Prosthesis seating and leaflet excursion.
- Transvalvular Doppler gradient, under appropriate flow.
- Paravalvular regurgitation.
- Coronary ostial obstruction.
- Ventricular function.
- Intracardiac air.

**Interpreting the gradient:**

- A high calculated gradient is flow-dependent.
- It may represent prosthesis–patient mismatch, excessive flow or measurement error.
- Interpret it with Doppler alignment, prosthesis type and size, and a baseline comparison.
- A new severe leak or a restricted leaflet is a surgical question.

**After surgery, watch for:**

- AV block.
- Atrial or ventricular arrhythmia.
- Bleeding.
- Early prosthetic dysfunction.
- Anticoagulation requirements.

### Choosing the prosthesis

**This is part of the anaesthetic story.**

- **Mechanical valves:**
  - Generally last longer.
  - Require lifelong VKA anticoagulation (not DOACs) with valve-specific INR targets.
- **Bioprostheses:**
  - Avoid lifelong VKA for the prosthesis alone.
  - Can degenerate.
  - May still need anticoagulation for AF or another indication.
- **Tissue choice is not decided by a single age cutoff.** It reflects lifetime intervention, patient preference, pregnancy plans, bleeding risk and ability to maintain a therapeutic INR.
- Source: [2025 ESC/EACTS valve guideline](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/44/4635/8234488).

### SAVR or TAVI?

The choice is individualised and made by the heart team. Anatomy, age and surgical risk decide most cases.

**Favours TAVI:**

- Older age. Guidelines place the age at which TAVI is preferred at roughly 70 to 80 years, and the threshold has fallen over time. For example, the 2025 ESC/EACTS guideline favours TAVI from about 70 years when transfemoral access is suitable, whereas the 2020 ACC/AHA guideline favours SAVR under 65, shared decision-making at 65 to 80, and TAVI above 80.
- High or prohibitive surgical risk, frailty or a limited life expectancy.
- A "hostile" chest or aorta: porcelain aorta, prior chest radiation, or a previous CABG with a patent graft (such as LIMA) lying behind the sternum.
- Severe lung, liver or renal disease, where CPB and sternotomy would be especially harmful.
- Suitable transfemoral access and a native annulus, root and coronary heights that suit a transcatheter valve.

**Favours SAVR:**

- Younger age, with a long life expectancy. Surgical bioprostheses and mechanical valves have long-term durability data; TAVI long-term durability and reintervention are still being defined.
- Another operation is needed at the same time: CABG, mitral or tricuspid surgery, or ascending aorta or root disease.
- Anatomy unsuitable for TAVI: bicuspid valve with a dilated aorta or heavy calcification, annulus too small or too large, low coronary ostial heights, LV or aortic root thrombus, or severe aortic root disease.
- Active endocarditis.
- Pure or predominant severe AR, because a transcatheter valve has no calcium to anchor against.
- Patient preference for a durable valve, or a mechanical valve.

**Trade-offs in practice:**

- **SAVR:** sternotomy and CPB, with more bleeding, AKI and new AF, and a longer recovery.
- **TAVI:** less invasive and faster recovery, but more pacemaker requirement, paravalvular leak and vascular complications, and a stroke risk. Future coronary access can be difficult, and a later valve-in-valve procedure depends on the first valve.
- **For the anaesthetist:** TAVI is often done under sedation or light general anaesthesia with rapid ventricular pacing, but CPB and surgical rescue must be available, so the team plans for conversion to open surgery.

## Mitral valve repair and replacement

### The valve and the two operations

- The mitral valve comprises leaflets, annulus, chordae and papillary muscles. Together they maintain competence and LV geometry.
- **Repair** is often preferred for suitable degenerative MR:
  - An annuloplasty ring reshapes and supports the annulus.
  - The surgeon restores leaflet closure, sometimes by restoring chordal support.
- **Replacement** implants a prosthesis while preserving the chordal apparatus where feasible.
- For anaesthesia, the important distinction is how each operation restores forward flow, changes LV loading, and can leave residual MR, stenosis or dynamic LVOT obstruction.

### Surgical sequence

- **1.** Establish CPB and cardioplegic arrest.
- **2.** Open the left atrium to access the mitral valve.
- **3.** Repair or replace the valve.
- **4.** Close the atrium, de-air, unclamp and reperfuse.
- **5.** Use TOE to assess the result at representative preload, afterload and heart rate.

TOE assesses:

- Valve closure and regurgitation.
- Transmitral gradient.
- Pulmonary venous flow.
- Ventricular function and the LV outflow tract.

Significant residual MR, an excessive transmitral gradient, systolic anterior motion (SAM), injury or prosthetic dysfunction may require another period of bypass and surgical correction.

### Mitral stenosis before surgery

- Impaired LA emptying raises LA, pulmonary venous and sometimes pulmonary arterial pressures. The RV may be chronically pressure-loaded.
- Tachycardia increases the diastolic transmitral gradient.
- AF can produce both low flow and rapid pulmonary congestion.
- Aim for:
  - A controlled rate and sinus rhythm when possible.
  - Adequate but not excessive filling.
  - Avoidance of hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis, which raise PVR.
- Pressure gradients are flow- and rate-dependent. Do not interpret an isolated number without the valve area, rhythm and clinical context.

### Mitral regurgitation before surgery

- The LV ejects into both the aorta and the low-resistance LA.
- The measured LVEF may appear preserved because some ejection is backwards. **An EF around 60% may already represent impaired LV function in severe chronic primary MR.**
- Avoid excessive afterload and bradycardia while preserving forward output.
- Pulmonary hypertension, RV dysfunction and AF are important risk modifiers.

### Immediately after correction

- The LV can no longer offload into the LA, so effective impedance to ejection increases.
- A stunned or previously decompensated LV may now fail (afterload mismatch) despite a technically satisfactory repair. Distinguish this on TOE from residual MR or coronary injury.
- **SAM-associated LVOTO:**
  - Suspect it when, after repair, there is a small hyperdynamic LV with anterior leaflet motion towards the septum, an LVOT gradient and posteriorly directed MR.
  - Reduce provoking contractility and tachycardia, restore afterload and correct genuine underfilling.
  - Consider surgical revision. Do not give reflex high-dose inotropes.
- When replacing a calcified or rheumatic valve, anticipate atrioventricular groove injury, circumflex coronary compromise and residual obstruction.

### Reassessment and the ICU baseline

- Reassess at physiological pressure, volume and rate.
- TOE must document:
  - Residual MR.
  - Functional mitral stenosis and the mean diastolic gradient.
  - SAM and the LVOT gradient.
  - LV and RV function.
  - Prosthesis seating where relevant.
- Persistent severe dysfunction or repair-related obstruction may require an early return to CPB for surgical correction.
- At the end, document residual regurgitation, gradients, ventricular function and rhythm as the ICU baseline.

items.title: 4. Cardiopulmonary bypass
items.body:
## What a cardiopulmonary bypass circuit does

CPB is a **temporary extracorporeal cardiopulmonary circulation**.

- Systemic venous blood passes via right atrial (two-stage) or bicaval cannulae to a venous reservoir.
- A roller or centrifugal pump propels blood through a membrane oxygenator and heat exchanger.
- Blood returns via an arterial filter and cannula, usually into the ascending aorta.
- Suction, vent and cardioplegia systems are supplementary circuits. Their contents, gas exchange and air risk need special attention.

![The CPB circuit: venous drainage, arterial return and cardioplegia · JTCVS Open](set13-c4-g1.jpg)

| Component                               | Function                                                         | Failure / exam implication                                                                                                                                |
|-----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Venous drainage/reservoir               | Receives venous return; buffers volume and allows air separation | Poor drainage from cannula obstruction, air lock, malposition, hypovolaemia or inadequate height/vacuum; low reservoir = air risk.                        |
| Pump                                    | Generates systemic flow independently of native ventricles       | Roller pumps are positive-displacement; centrifugal output depends on preload/afterload and may permit reverse flow if mismanaged.                        |
| Membrane oxygenator + sweep gas         | Adds O₂ and removes CO₂                                          | **Blood flow** predominantly determines systemic O₂ delivery; **sweep-gas rate** mainly controls CO₂ removal; oxygenator FiO₂/area influence O₂ transfer. |
| Heat exchanger                          | Cools/warms blood                                                | Avoid large gradients, hyperthermia and gaseous microemboli; multiple temperatures required.                                                              |
| Arterial filter/air detector            | Reduces particles and bubbles                                    | Air embolisation remains catastrophic if reservoir empties or line is compromised.                                                                        |
| Cardioplegia / LV and aortic root vents | Arrests myocardium and prevents distension/air                   | Incorrect delivery, obstruction or inadequate venting causes ischaemia/LV distension and later failure to wean.                                           |

### Mean arterial pressure on bypass

- MAP depends on pump flow and systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
- Many centres aim for roughly **50–80 mmHg**, individualised for cerebrovascular disease, autoregulation, metabolic need and high-risk organs. Evidence does not justify one universal high MAP target.
- Lack of pulsatility does not necessarily mean absent perfusion.
- A low MAP with adequate flow, oxygen delivery and reassuring monitoring may simply be low SVR.
- Low flow with a reassuring MAP can still be dangerous.
- Avoid raising pressure with vasoconstrictors before confirming adequate blood flow.

## The three dials the perfusionist controls

- **Blood flow:** litres per minute around the body. This is a major determinant of oxygen delivery.
- **Oxygenator FiO₂:** how well the blood is oxygenated in the membrane.
- **Sweep-gas flow:** how much CO₂ is washed away.
- Turning up sweep is a CO₂ manoeuvre. It is not a substitute for increasing blood flow.
- The heat exchanger is a fourth control, for cooling and rewarming.
- Increasing oxygenator FiO₂ cannot compensate for low pump flow, and increasing sweep does not raise the haemoglobin concentration.

## Circuit engineering, cannulation and priming

### Venous drainage and cannulae

- A **two-stage cannula** drains IVC and right atrial blood through separate openings in one cannula.
- **Bicaval drainage** cannulates the SVC and IVC individually and allows caval snares when the right atrium must be opened.
- Drainage is normally driven by gravity (height difference) and may be augmented by regulated reservoir vacuum.
- Excess negative pressure risks venous collapse, air entrainment, haemolysis and gaseous microemboli.
- A small or kinked cannula sharply increases resistance. In laminar flow, resistance varies inversely with radius to the fourth power, although actual cannula pressure loss may be turbulent.
- Poor return limits pump output even when the pump itself is working.

### Pumps, oxygenator and heat exchanger

- **Roller pumps** periodically occlude flexible tubing. Output is approximately displacement per revolution × rate, so a downstream obstruction can create extreme pressure until a safety limit intervenes.
- **Centrifugal pumps** use a rotating impeller. Delivered flow depends on speed, inlet pressure and downstream resistance, not RPM alone. They need a flowmeter and safe prevention of retrograde flow when stopping or weaning.
- The **hollow-fibre membrane oxygenator** separates blood from gas, so diffusion occurs with limited direct blood–gas contact. High membrane resistance, gas failure or clot burden can compromise exchange.
- The **heat exchanger** transfers heat without mixing water and blood.

### Cardioplegia, suction and vents

- Cardioplegia is a separate, controlled delivery circuit.
- Suction recovers blood from the surgical field, and vents decompress the left heart.
- Suctioned blood can contain air, fat, activated coagulation products and tissue debris.

### Priming and haemodilution

- The circuit is primed with crystalloid or colloid, which dilutes red cells, clotting factors and platelets.
- **Worked example:** a 70 kg adult has an estimated blood volume of 70 mL/kg = 4.9 L, pre-CPB Hct 0.36 and a 1.5 L crystalloid prime.
  - Ignoring losses and redistribution, post-prime Hct = 0.36 × 4.9 / 6.4 = 0.276 (27.6%).
  - A smaller patient, or extra crystalloid or cardioplegia, causes proportionally more dilution.
- Ways to limit dilution: reduced prime, retrograde autologous priming in suitable patients, and selected haemoconcentration.
- **Ultrafiltration** drives plasma water across a semipermeable membrane under a transmembrane pressure gradient. It concentrates cells and retained proteins but does not repair platelet dysfunction or guarantee better outcomes.

## Pump flow, pressure and oxygen delivery

### Oxygen delivery: what the terms mean

- **Oxygen delivery (DO₂)** is the amount of oxygen the pump delivers to the body each minute. Its unit is mL/min.
- **DO₂i** is DO₂ indexed to body surface area (BSA), which is the same value divided by BSA. Its unit is mL/min/m².
  - Indexing allows for body size, so a small and a large patient can be compared against one target.
  - Pump flow is indexed in the same way: **flow index** (L/min/m²) = pump flow (L/min) ÷ BSA (m²).
- **CaO₂** is the arterial oxygen content: the oxygen carried in each dL of blood, mostly bound to haemoglobin.
- **Q** is pump flow in L/min.

### The equations

- **CaO₂** (mL/dL) = 1.34 × Hb (g/dL) × SaO₂ (fraction) + 0.023 × PaO₂ (kPa).
  - The first term is oxygen bound to haemoglobin. The second is dissolved oxygen, which is small.
- **DO₂** (mL/min) = 10 × Q (L/min) × CaO₂ (mL/dL).
  - The factor of 10 converts mL/dL to mL/L.
- **DO₂i** (mL/min/m²) = 10 × flow index (L/min/m²) × CaO₂ (mL/dL).
  - This is the same as DO₂ ÷ BSA.
- **Oxygen extraction ratio** = (CaO₂ − CvO₂) / CaO₂, where CvO₂ is the venous oxygen content.

### Worked example: calculating DO₂i

- Hb 80 g/L, SaO₂ 1.0 and PaO₂ 20 kPa give CaO₂ = 10.72 + 0.46 = 11.18 mL/dL.
- At a flow of 2.4 L/min/m², DO₂i ≈ 268 mL/min/m².
- To reach 280 at that content needs a flow of about 2.50 L/min/m², if venous drainage and perfusion pressures allow.
- If you ignore the dissolved oxygen term (0.023 × PaO₂), DO₂i is about 257 mL/min/m². The difference is small, so either method is acceptable in an answer, but say which one you used.
- A MAP of 70 does not ensure adequate delivery.

### Flow targets

- **Typical adult flow** starts around **2.2–2.6 L/min/m²** at normothermia, adjusted for temperature, metabolic needs, Hb, venous saturation, lactate and clinical conditions.
- The 2024 European CPB guideline recommends goal-directed perfusion that limits time at low DO₂.
- It suggests a lower indexed DO₂ threshold of about **280–300 mL/min/m² during normothermic CPB**, to reduce early AKI risk.
- This is a practical target, not an absolute individual survival cutoff, and measurement methods vary.
- Do not treat the usual flow index as a substitute for patient-specific oxygen delivery.
- Source: [2024 CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/).

### Variables to follow together

- Circuit flow and arterial line pressure.
- Calculated indexed DO₂.
- Haemoglobin and haematocrit.
- Arterial and venous gases, and SvO₂.
- Temperature.
- Lactate trend and urine output.
- Regional cerebral oximetry (NIRS), where used.

### Interpreting the numbers

- **Falling venous saturation** can mean increasing extraction from inadequate DO₂, high metabolic demand (for example during rewarming), a sample or monitor fault, or shunting.
  - Interpret it alongside the other variables rather than transfusing automatically.
- During complete CPB a representative venous sample reflects global extraction, but shunting, sampling position and altered metabolism confound it.
- **A rising lactate** can reflect oxygen debt, catecholamine-enhanced glycolysis or impaired hepatic clearance.
- A normal lactate early in malperfusion does not exclude regional ischaemia.

### Worked troubleshooting: low delivery despite a normal MAP

- BSA 1.8 m², pump flow 3.6 L/min (2.0 L/min/m²), Hb 70 g/L, SaO₂ 100%, PaO₂ 20 kPa: CaO₂ ≈ 9.84 mL/dL and DO₂i ≈ 197 mL/min/m².
- A MAP of 70 mmHg does not correct this low delivery.
- **Steps:**
  - Check cannula drainage, reservoir and circuit.
  - Safely increase flow if possible.
  - Assess haemodilution, extraction, NIRS and lactate before choosing haemoconcentration or red cell transfusion.
- If flow and delivery are adequate but MAP is low, assess SVR and titrate a vasopressor.
- Source: 2024 adult CPB guideline (published 2025).

## PaCO₂, pH and temperature: what the perfusionist is controlling

- The oxygenator gas blender determines oxygen transfer, the gas sweep largely determines CO₂ clearance, and the pump sets systemic blood flow.
- PaCO₂ matters because it alters cerebral arteriolar tone and cerebral blood flow.

### Alpha-stat

- Analyses arterial blood gases as measured at 37°C, without temperature-correcting the target.
- At hypothermia, in-vivo PaCO₂ is lower and pH higher than the displayed 37°C value.
- This tends to preserve cerebral autoregulation and protein charge state.
- Commonly used in adult CPB, especially when atheroembolism risk is important.

### pH-stat

- Adds CO₂ during cooling so that the temperature-corrected pH is about 7.40 and PaCO₂ about 40 mmHg.
- Cerebral vasodilatation increases flow and cooling uniformity, but potentially also the distribution of gaseous and particulate emboli.
- Used selectively in paediatric and some deep-cooling contexts, not as a universal adult default.

## Haemodilution, inflammation and the body's response

**The overall message:** bypass exposes the blood to things it never meets normally. The result is a whole-body inflammatory, leaky and bleeding-prone state. That is why patients often come off bypass vasodilated, oedematous and oozing, and why some develop kidney, lung or brain injury.

### Two things happen to the blood

- **Dilution:** the crystalloid or colloid prime dilutes red cells, clotting factors and platelets.
- **Contact and injury:** blood meets artificial tubing, suctioned mediastinal blood, surgical trauma and reperfusion. These switch on the contact, complement, cytokine and coagulation pathways.
  - Contact activation involves factor XII and kallikrein.
  - Complement activation involves C3a and C5a.
  - Tissue factor exposure, neutrophil activation and cytokine release amplify each other.

### What this does, and what you see

- **Vessels: leak and vasoplegia.**
  - Endothelial barrier disruption causes capillary leak and interstitial oedema.
  - Nitric oxide-mediated vasodilatation causes vasoplegia.
  - **You see:** low SVR needing a vasopressor, and fluid shifting out of the circulation into the tissues.
- **Blood: bleeding.**
  - Platelet adhesion to surfaces, receptor dysfunction, mechanical shear and hypothermia impair primary haemostasis.
  - Consumption, dilution and plasmin activation impair secondary haemostasis.
  - **You see:** microvascular oozing and a coagulopathy after protamine.
- **Red cells: haemolysis.**
  - Free haemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, promotes oxidative injury and can injure renal tubules.
  - **You see:** pigmented urine, and a contribution to AKI.
- **Kidney:** vulnerable to low DO₂, haemolysis, inflammation, venous congestion and pre-existing CKD.
- **Lung:** ischaemia–reperfusion, inflammatory permeability and transfusion can cause postoperative gas exchange failure.
- **Brain:** injury comes from embolism (air or atheroma), hypoperfusion and inflammatory or metabolic factors, not a single mechanism.

### Temperature

- **Cooling** reduces metabolic demand, but it also slows enzyme and drug clearance, alters coagulation and shifts the oxyhaemoglobin curve.
- **Rewarming** raises metabolic demand again.
- Apparent stability while cold can hide inadequate oxygen delivery, so watch SvO₂ and lactate as the patient warms.

### What this means for perfusion

- The aim is a balance of **adequate oxygen delivery, avoiding emboli, temperature control and avoiding unnecessary blood–surface exposure**.
- Routine high-dose steroid prophylaxis has not improved major outcomes (SIRS/DECS), so it is not a standard fix.

## Initiating CPB safely: a closed-loop communication sequence

- **1.** Confirm circuit checks, oxygen source and sweep, priming, arterial line and pressure monitoring, air management, blood availability, cannulation plan and emergency backup.
- **2.** Give systemic heparin and **verify adequate anticoagulation** before any CPB flow (details and ACT limitations are in Chapter 5).
- **3.** With direct surgeon–perfusionist–anaesthetist communication, confirm arterial and venous cannula placement and perfusion pressure. Start venous drainage and pump flow gradually, watching reservoir level, MAP, air detectors and venous pressures.
- **4.** Transition ventilation and anaesthesia to on-bypass practice.
  - Lung ventilation may be reduced or stopped by agreement, while the oxygenator manages oxygen delivery and CO₂ clearance.
  - Ensure an explicit **IV or volatile anaesthetic delivery route** to prevent awareness as pulmonary uptake changes.
- **5.** Maintain indexed flow, temperature and gas exchange. Monitor ACT, ABG, haematocrit, lactate, NIRS and urine output, and communicate haemodynamic and cerebral concerns regularly.

## Anaesthesia during CPB

### Maintaining anaesthesia

- The lungs may no longer exchange much gas with the systemic circulation, so **volatile agents delivered only into the ventilator may not maintain anaesthesia**.
- Options: volatile agent through an appropriately designed, scavenged oxygenator vapour system, or an IV infusion.
- Monitor gas delivery with the perfusionist, not the ventilator display alone.
- Neuromuscular blockade prevents movement but does not prevent awareness.
- Use a clear infusion or vaporiser plan, consistent pump checks and processed EEG where appropriate.
- EEG changes with hypothermia and circulatory arrest. BIS may read very low when cold even without a proportionate change in hypnotic delivery.
- **MYRIAD** found no 1-year survival advantage for volatile anaesthesia over TIVA in elective isolated CABG. Choose reliable delivery and patient physiology rather than presumed outcome superiority.

### Pharmacokinetics on bypass

- Concentrations and clinical response change with haemodilution, protein binding, circuit sequestration, altered cerebral blood flow and hypothermia.
- An initial dilutional fall in plasma concentration does not necessarily mean a lower free drug concentration, because haemodilution also lowers albumin and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein.
- Hypothermia slows hepatic metabolism and renal clearance.
- Circuit tubing can adsorb lipophilic agents.
- During rewarming, distribution, clearance and drug requirements change again.

### Ventilation

- Local strategies range from apnoea with low-level CPAP to low tidal-volume ventilation. Outcome evidence does not support one universal method.
- Before separation, recruit gently, re-establish oxygenation and ventilation, and avoid excessive airway pressure that would compromise RV output.
- Always agree switching the ventilator off and on with perfusion and surgery.

## Complications during bypass: recognise the mechanism

- **Circuit clotting:** from inadequate anticoagulation. Maintain perfusion safety, obtain ACT and heparin measurements, and change circuit components if required.
- **Unexpected cerebral NIRS fall:**
  - Exclude sensor or technical failure.
  - Assess pump flow, MAP, Hb, PaCO₂, SaO₂, cannula or arch-vessel malperfusion and temperature.
  - Address each cause rather than assuming isolated hypotension.
- **Falling post-oxygenator PaO₂ or rising PaCO₂ despite adequate pump flow:**
  - Check gas supply, blender FiO₂, sweep tubing and gas flow.
  - Confirm pre- and post-oxygenator blood samples and the pressure gradient across the membrane.
  - If gas exchange or membrane integrity cannot be restored, prepare a controlled oxygenator or circuit exchange with perfusion.
  - Maintain anaesthesia and anticoagulation during troubleshooting.

## Three dangerous technical emergencies on CPB

### 1. Inadequate venous drainage

- The arterial pump may deliver more blood than returns to the reservoir. The reservoir falls, and systemic air entry becomes a catastrophe.
- **Immediately:** alert the perfusionist and surgeon, and reduce output as needed to preserve circuit safety.
- **Check:** cannula position and kinking, venous obstruction, excessive suction or vacuum-assisted drainage, patient positioning and true volume depletion.
- A low CVP is not diagnostic when the venous cannula actively drains the atrium.
- Repositioning the cannula or correcting the obstruction may restore drainage more effectively than giving fluid.

### 2. Arterial line obstruction or malperfusion

**Two different "arterial" pressures:**

- **CPB arterial line pressure** is measured inside the bypass circuit, between the pump/oxygenator and the aortic cannula. It shows how hard the pump is pushing blood into the cannula. The perfusionist watches it.
- **Systemic arterial pressure** is the patient's own pressure, from your radial or femoral arterial line. It shows what actually reaches the patient.
- Normally the circuit pressure is higher than the patient's, because blood loses pressure squeezing through the narrow aortic cannula.
- The two move apart when something between the gauge and the aorta blocks flow.

**Pattern:**

- Circuit arterial line pressure **rises** while the patient's systemic pressure **falls**.
- The pump is pushing against a blockage, so less blood reaches the patient.
- Possible causes: a kinked or clamped line, an arterial cannula obstruction or malposition (for example the tip against the aortic wall), or cannulation into the false lumen of an aortic dissection.
- Cannulating into a dissection can deliver flow into the false lumen and compromise cerebral and visceral perfusion.

**Immediately:**

- Stop unsafe escalation of pump pressure, and communicate with the perfusionist and surgeon.
- Check the line and cannula, bilateral arterial pressures (radial or femoral) and NIRS.
- TOE or imaging, or direct surgical assessment, and a new arterial cannulation plan may be required.

### 3. Massive air entry into the arterial circuit

- Treat this as a team emergency, not a routine brief "air bubble".
- Follow the perfusion emergency protocol to prevent further air delivery.
- Secure the arterial line, stop or manage pump flow appropriately, and identify and correct the source.
- Use circuit air-handling and filtration procedures.
- The surgeon assesses aortic root and cerebral or coronary de-airing strategies.
- Prolonged unperfused time can be worse than the air event, so rapid, coordinated restoration of safe flow is critical.
- Clinical neurological injury may appear only after rewarming or awakening.

Source: [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/).

items.title: 5. Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.los: SS_CS 1.17 (anticoagulation, point-of-care testing, antifibrinolytics, protamine); SS_CS 1.18 (heparin resistance and HIT)
items.body:
## The clotting system before learning ACT, heparin resistance and ROTEM

A stable clot needs **platelets** to form an initial plug, **coagulation factors** to generate thrombin, **fibrinogen** to become strong fibrin strands, and a balance against **fibrinolysis** (clot breakdown). Cardiac surgery interferes with all four: bypass dilutes factors and platelets, artificial surfaces and suction activate clotting/inflammation, hypothermia slows enzymes, and the surgical field can bleed independently of the laboratory results. These processes explain why replacing just one blood product cannot solve every case.

## Why standard coagulation is inadequate for bypass

The CPB circuit exposes blood to foreign surfaces and high shear; without anticoagulation, fibrin and platelet deposition may obstruct the oxygenator or arterial circuit and precipitate catastrophic embolism. **Unfractionated heparin (UFH)** is preferred because it acts rapidly, can be monitored at bedside and is antagonised by protamine. Heparin potentiates **antithrombin (AT)** inhibition of thrombin (IIa) and Xa, with effects on several other serine proteases. Its effect depends on adequate antithrombin, heparin-binding proteins and patient response.

A common initial CPB heparin dose is **300–400 units/kg IV**, but the correct target is adequate anticoagulation on the chosen circuit/test, not a universally fixed number of units. Many conventional adult CPB services use **ACT >480 seconds** before cannulation and throughout; some use lower device-specific thresholds for heparin-coated circuits, different ACT technology or alternative protocols. Recheck after heparin, during prolonged CPB and when additional anticoagulant is given. A surprisingly high ACT may reflect hypothermia, haemodilution, thrombocytopenia or test artefact rather than sufficient true heparin activity.

## Plan haemostasis before the first heparin dose

Cardiac-surgical bleeding is difficult because **three problems overlap**: a surgeon may have an unligated vessel; CPB can consume/dilute/impair the haemostatic system; and the patient may already be receiving antithrombotic drugs. The correct approach is to anticipate all three rather than react to a large chest-drain output with indiscriminate plasma.

**Preoperative patient blood management** means evaluating anaemia and its cause (iron deficiency, CKD, inflammation or B12/folate deficiency), defining aspirin/P2Y12/warfarin/DOAC exposure and last dose, estimating bleeding risk from redo surgery/complex aortic procedures, and establishing a crossmatch/cell-salvage plan. Treat iron deficiency when scheduling permits; avoid transfusing an asymptomatic anaemic patient simply to obtain a normal Hb without considering risks and timing. A formal MDT decision is required when urgent ACS-related CABG conflicts with platelet-inhibitor washout. The 2024 EACTS/EACTAIC patient-blood-management guideline emphasises preoperative optimisation and patient-specific coagulation strategies. [Guideline](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae352).

**During the operation, reduce avoidable loss:** meticulous surgical haemostasis, minimally necessary bypass prime volume and haemodilution, cell salvage, suitable transfusion thresholds, normothermia, correction of hypocalcaemia and acidosis, and an antifibrinolytic strategy. Cell salvage does not reliably return platelets/coagulation factors; washed recovered RBCs improve oxygen-carrying capacity but do not replace targeted haemostatic therapy. The team must know whether autologous blood sequestered before CPB remains available for reinfusion after reversal.

## Monitoring: what the tests measure

| Test                                                  | What it tells you                                                                                        | Major limitations                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| ACT (activated clotting time)                         | Whole-blood clotting time after contact activator; rapid point-of-care assessment at high heparin levels | Altered by low platelets, low temperature, haemodilution, factors, device and activator; not a precise heparin concentration.  |
| Heparin concentration / anti-Xa                       | More direct assessment of heparin exposure/effect where available                                        | Methods and high-dose calibration differ; anti-Xa measures AT-dependent activity and may be less practical at full CPB levels. |
| aPTT                                                  | Helpful for conventional UFH outside CPB                                                                 | Saturates at high heparin levels; generally unsuitable as sole monitoring on CPB.                                              |
| TEG/ROTEM with heparinase comparison                  | Detects residual heparin and identifies fibrinogen/platelet/coagulation deficits during bleeding work-up | Not a substitute for adequately anticoagulating the circuit; VHA thresholds depend on cartridge and local algorithm.           |
| FBC, fibrinogen, PT/INR, ionised Ca, ABG, temperature | Interpret the patient’s capacity to clot after CPB                                                       | Laboratory turnaround and assay artefacts; treat clinical bleeding, not numerical abnormalities alone.                         |
