Resting HR is often around 90–110/min; stroke volume increases with venous return (Frank–Starling mechanism), while the HR response to exercise and circulating catecholamines is delayed. Partial reinnervation may develop over years, so drug responses are not universally absent.

![Donor and recipient anatomy and completed cardiac transplantation · BJA Education 2024](set13-c13-g1.png)

## Preoperative: know graft function and immunosuppression

- **Is the graft healthy?** Ask about timing of transplant, current exercise tolerance, rejection episodes, latest echo and transplant clinic review, rhythm/pacemaker history and cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV). Obtain further testing guided by symptoms, clinical change and transplant cardiologist. A normal EF is reassuring but does not exclude silent coronary disease.

- **Silent ischaemia matters:** CAV can cause graft ischaemia without typical angina because pain fibres are denervated. New fatigue, arrhythmia, reduced output or an unexplained ECG/echo change may represent ischaemia, rejection or other graft disease.

- **Medication and organ review:** immunosuppressants such as tacrolimus/ciclosporin, mycophenolate and steroids are usually continued with an appropriate fasting/alternative-route plan. Check renal function, blood count, potassium, magnesium, glucose, interacting antibiotics/antifungals and infection risk. Discuss major surgery with the transplant service.

## Intraoperative: denervated physiology changes rescue choices

- **Loading:** avoid abrupt large decreases in preload or SVR after induction/major neuraxial block. Do not interpret a fixed HR as adequate volume status or depth. Individualise fluids to actual output and function, since a failing graft can still be harmed by overload.

- **Vasoactive and chronotropic drugs:** direct-acting vasopressors/inotropes such as noradrenaline, phenylephrine and adrenaline work at their receptors. Ephedrine may have less predictable effect when it depends on releasing stored norepinephrine. Atropine and glycopyrrolate often have little chronotropic effect in an initially denervated heart; for profound bradycardia prepare direct-acting chronotropy (e.g. isoprenaline/adrenaline in the appropriate setting) and pacing. Delayed reinnervation means responses vary between recipients.

Other denervation implications: slow onset/offset of HR response to exercise via circulating catecholamines, attenuated Valsalva/baroreflex responses, and limited vagolytic effect of antimuscarinics. Adenosine may have an exaggerated AV-nodal effect; if used for a suitable SVT, use reduced initial dosing and monitoring with cardiology support. Neostigmine has caused severe bradycardia even years post-transplant; do not assume vagal blockade prevents it. Tailor reversal to neuromuscular monitoring and renal function; have pacing/direct chronotropy ready. CAV is diffuse coronary intimal disease, not just focal ordinary atherosclerosis; absence of angina does not exclude it.

- **Standard anaesthesia with special precautions:** choose GA or regional according to surgery, anticoagulation and graft health. Preserve asepsis and appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis; avoid renal insults and clinically important interactions with calcineurin inhibitors. Add invasive monitoring if major surgery or impaired graft reserve makes beat-to-beat physiology important.

## What pneumoperitoneum changes in a transplanted heart

In 2020.2 Q1 the examiner specifically highlighted pneumoperitoneum. Raised intra-abdominal pressure and reverse Trendelenburg may reduce venous return. Insufflation can raise SVR and airway pressures. Carbon dioxide absorption can increase PaCO₂ and PVR. Attenuated immediate chronotropy and limited graft reserve can magnify the fall in output. Review graft and RV function, titrate insufflation and position, maintain ventilation and agree when to desufflate. Have direct-acting vasoactive drugs and pacing available.

[ANZCA exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [ISHLT heart transplant recipient guidance](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37080658/)

## Postoperative: protect the transplanted heart

- **Restart immunosuppression promptly** with transplant-team guidance and level monitoring where appropriate; monitor renal function, glucose, electrolytes, wounds and infection (which may present atypically). Steroid stress dosing depends on adrenal suppression and chronic exposure, not transplant status alone.

- **New hypotension, arrhythmia, low cardiac output or pulmonary oedema:** investigate ordinary surgical causes alongside rejection, CAV-related ischaemia and graft dysfunction; obtain ECG/echo and specialist input rather than assuming a normal resting HR excludes deterioration.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
## Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation

- **[CORONARY — Lamy et al., NEJM 2016, five-year follow-up](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1601564).** 4,752 patients randomised to off- versus on-pump CABG. The five-year composite of death, stroke, MI, renal failure or repeat revascularisation was **23.1% versus 23.6%** (no significant difference). Use: operator experience, completeness of grafting and patient anatomy are important; off-pump is not uniformly safer.
- **[ROOBY five-year follow-up — Shroyer et al., NEJM 2017](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1614341).** In a largely male veteran population, five-year death was **15.2% off pump versus 11.9% on pump**. Use: apparently less invasive strategies can produce inferior long-term outcomes in certain contexts; do not generalise one trial to every centre.
- **[GOPCABE — Diegeler et al., NEJM 2013](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1211666).** Elderly patients (≥75 years) having CABG: no major difference in primary composite outcomes at 30 days, although repeat revascularisation differed. Use: the operative method is not chosen on age alone.
- **[ATACAS tranexamic acid — Myles et al., NEJM 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27774838/).** TXA in coronary surgery reduced blood product use (4,331 vs 7,994 units total) and reoperation for major haemorrhage/tamponade (1.4% vs 2.8%) **but increased seizures** (0.7% vs 0.1%). No statistically significant improvement in its primary composite thrombotic/death outcome. Use: give TXA for blood conservation with a sensible, renal-adjusted dose; seizures are dose/context related.
- **[TRICS III — Mazer et al., NEJM 2017](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1711818).** 4,860 moderate/high-risk cardiac surgical patients; restrictive RBC transfusion trigger **Hb 7.5 g/dL** was non-inferior to liberal transfusion for death, MI, stroke and new dialysis (11.4% vs 12.5%). Use: restrictive transfusion is reasonable in stable patients; reassess active haemorrhage and ischaemia individually.
- **[TRICS III six-month follow-up — Mazer et al., NEJM 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30146969/).** Noninferiority of restrictive strategy persisted for the composite clinical outcome at six months. Use: reinforces that using less blood did not worsen the trial’s specified outcomes.
- **[TITRe2 — Murphy et al., NEJM 2015](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1403612).** Postoperative cardiac surgical patients allocated to different restrictive/liberal transfusion thresholds: no significant difference in the primary serious infection/ischaemic composite, but a mortality signal favoured the liberal group, creating earlier uncertainty. Use: contextualise subsequent TRICS III rather than pretending all cardiac transfusion evidence is identical.
- **[BART — Fergusson et al., NEJM 2008](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0802395).** Compared antifibrinolytic agents in high-risk cardiac surgery; aprotinin associated with concerning mortality compared with lysine analogues. Use: the choice of antifibrinolytic is a safety decision; policy/regulatory status varies by jurisdiction.
- **[SIRS trial — Whitlock et al., Lancet 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26460660/).** 7,507 patients on CPB randomised to methylprednisolone versus placebo: no reduction in 30-day mortality or major morbidity. Use: routine prophylactic high-dose corticosteroid is not an evidence-based default for CPB-related inflammatory response.
- **[DECS — Dieleman et al., JAMA 2012](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.14144).** High-dose dexamethasone in cardiac surgery did not significantly improve its composite major-adverse-event primary outcome, despite some secondary differences. Use: avoid translating anti-inflammatory biomarker changes into assured clinical benefit.
- **[TRACS — Hajjar et al., JAMA 2010](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.1446).** Compared restrictive versus liberal transfusion based on haematocrit after cardiac surgery, finding no significant composite outcome difference in its sample. Use: original transfusion evidence is limited by selected patients, thresholds and statistical power.
- **FARES-II** (2025; 420 treated patients): multicentre randomised comparison of four-factor PCC versus frozen plasma for factor-related bleeding after CPB. Haemostatic effectiveness 77.9% versus 60.4%; fewer blood components with PCC. Open-label treatment and selected bleeding population limit universal extrapolation; not a substitute for fibrinogen, platelets or surgical haemostasis. [Publication](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.3501)
- **FIBRES** (2019; 735 treated patients): fibrinogen concentrate 4 g versus 10 Canadian units of cryoprecipitate for clinically significant post-CPB bleeding/hypofibrinogenaemia. Mean 24-hour transfusion 16.3 versus 17.0 units; noninferiority demonstrated, not superiority. Product availability and local unit definitions matter. [Publication](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2753529)
- **OPTIMAL** (2022): randomised high versus low TXA dosing during on-pump cardiac surgery. Higher dose modestly reduced RBC transfusion; composite safety met the prespecified noninferiority margin, but seizures remain an important concern. Renal clearance, open-chamber surgery and external applicability matter. [Publication](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2022.10725)
- **MYRIAD** (2019; 5,400 patients): pragmatic trial of volatile-containing anaesthesia versus TIVA in elective isolated CABG; no significant reduction in 1-year mortality with volatile agents. Does not establish equivalent outcomes in every emergency or complex valve procedure; reliable anaesthetic delivery is crucial. [Publication](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1816476)
- **ERICCA** (2015; 1,612 high-risk patients): remote ischaemic preconditioning versus sham before on-pump CABG ± valve surgery; no significant improvement in the 12-month composite clinical endpoint. Mechanistic cardioprotection should not be equated with proven clinical benefit. [Publication](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1413534)
- **GIFT** (2018; 350 enrolled): goal-directed perfusion targeting DO₂i ≥280 versus conventional perfusion. Reduced stage 1 AKI, without established reduction in more severe AKI; target is a useful approach and not an isolated transfusion trigger. [Publication](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29778331/)
- **VANCS** (2017): randomised vasopressin versus noradrenaline in post-cardiac-surgery vasoplegic shock. Vasopressin reduced the composite of death/severe complications in this single-centre trial; evidence does not establish universal superiority for all hypotensive postoperative patients. [Publication](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27841822/)
- **PROTECTION** (2024; 3,511 patients): IV balanced amino acids (2 g/kg ideal body weight/day, up to 3 days) versus Ringer’s placebo during/after cardiac surgery with CPB. AKI 26.9% versus 31.7% (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.77–0.94). Creatinine-defined benefit does not establish survival or dialysis benefit; protocol and population matter. [Publication](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2403769)

## Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support

- **[IABP-SHOCK II — Thiele et al., NEJM 2012; follow-up](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24011548/).** Around 600 patients with MI-related cardiogenic shock and planned early revascularisation: routine IABP did **not** lower 30-day or one-year mortality. Use: indications for IABP now focus on selected bridging physiology rather than a universal survival benefit.
- **[DanGer Shock — Møller et al., NEJM 2024](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2312572).** Selected STEMI-related shock patients: Impella CP decreased 180-day mortality **45.8% vs 58.5%**, but increased severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis and renal replacement. Use: selected phenotype and procedure expertise are central; do not apply indiscriminately to postcardiotomy patients.
- **[ECLS-SHOCK — Thiele et al., NEJM 2023](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227).** Early VA-ECMO for infarct-related shock did not improve 30-day mortality (**47.8% vs 49.0%**); more bleeding and vascular complications. Use: ‘more flow’ does not guarantee improved survival and imposes a complication burden.
- **[ECMO-CS — Ošťádal et al., Circulation 2023](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.122.062949).** Immediate VA-ECMO versus early conservative management with rescue ECMO in rapidly deteriorating severe cardiogenic shock; no clear improvement in the primary composite clinical outcome from immediate routine ECMO. Use: timely selected rescue rather than automatic cannulation.
- **[SHOCK — Hochman et al., NEJM 1999](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199908263410901).** Early coronary revascularisation in MI-associated cardiogenic shock improved longer-term outcomes even though the 30-day primary mortality difference was not statistically significant. Use: definitive correction of ischaemia remains fundamental; support devices are bridges.

## VV-ECMO for respiratory failure

- **[CESAR — Peek et al., Lancet 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19762075/).** Randomised **referral to an ECMO-capable centre**, not ECMO itself in every patient: 63% versus 47% survived without severe disability at six months. Use: supports specialist service organisation/referral but does not isolate the benefit of the pump alone.
- **[EOLIA — Combes et al., NEJM 2018](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1800385).** Severe ARDS: 60-day mortality **35% ECMO versus 46% control**, P=0.09 for prespecified primary comparison; 28% crossed over from control to rescue ECMO. Use: important signal underpowered/interpreted with crossover, not a definitive positive primary mortality trial.

## Recovery and postoperative haemodynamics

- **[ERAS Cardiac Society consensus — Engelman et al., JAMA Surgery 2019](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamasurg.2019.1153).** Evidence-based expert recommendations for bundled cardiac enhanced recovery, including prehabilitation, opioid-sparing analgesia, glycaemic control and early mobilisation. Use: fast tracking is a pathway, not just extubation speed; this is consensus and mixed-level evidence rather than one mortality RCT.
- **[Temporary epicardial pacing — BJA Education 2023 clinical review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.003).** Not a landmark trial, but a high-yield illustrated teaching publication on pacing modes, threshold checks, capture/sensing and postoperative safety. Use: directly supports practical weaning and the 2026.1 examiner-style pacing question.
- **[2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae354).** High-impact evidence synthesis rather than a clinical trial: perfusion, temperature, neurological protection, circuit safety, anticoagulation and myocardial protection. Use: this is the best contemporary synthesis for the technical CPB sections.

items.title: References by subtopic
items.body:
## BJA Education reading guide: what to read and why

- **[Principles of cardiopulmonary bypass](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/6/5/176/337119)** (BJA Education, 2006). **Start here for the circuit.** Older but exceptionally useful for how venous drainage, pump, oxygenator, heat exchange and cannulation actually work; update practice thresholds from the 2024 CPB guideline.
- **[Anticoagulation for cardiopulmonary bypass: part one — Cartwright & Mundell](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003)** (BJA Education, 2023). **Highest-yield for heparin, ACT, resistance, rebound and protamine.** Read with the anticoagulation chapter and repeat the protamine-reaction differential aloud.
- **[Anticoagulation for cardiopulmonary bypass: part two — Cartwright & Mundell](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.03.008)** (BJA Education, 2023). **Highest-yield for HIT and alternatives to heparin.** Particularly useful for distinguishing expected post-CPB thrombocytopenia from HIT and managing bivalirudin on bypass.
- **[Temporary epicardial pacing after cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.003)** (BJA Education, 2023). **Essential for pacing, weaning and ICU capture troubleshooting**; directly relevant to recent ANZCA questions.
- **[Anaesthesia for adult cardiac surgery requiring repeat sternotomy](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.10.001)** (BJA Education, 2024). **Best set-specific reading for SS_CS 1.15**: CT, previous grafts, emergency access, pre-sternotomy CPB and haemorrhage.
- **[Perioperative care in cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.05.008)** (BJA Education, 2021). **Best for fast-track/ERAS concepts**, sedation, analgesia, mobilisation and recovery care.
- **[Veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in severe acute respiratory failure](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.01.001)** (BJA Education, 2024). **Practical VV-ECMO overview**: referral, indications, oxygenation/sweep, ventilation and weaning.
- **[Physiology of VV-ECMO, Part 1: terminology, circuits and gas exchange](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.003)** (BJA Education, 2026). **Best newer physiology-focused follow-up**; useful for explaining recirculation, blood-flow versus sweep effects and oxygen delivery.
- **[Management of cardiogenic shock after acute coronary syndromes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.01.006)** (BJA Education, 2023). **Use for MCS physiology** and the distinction between revascularisation, pressors/inotropy and device-supported circulatory rescue; update device trial interpretation using DanGer Shock/ECLS-SHOCK.
- **[Anaesthesia for minimally invasive cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2018.06.004)** (BJA Education, 2018). **Useful for procedure variations, cannulation, positioning and TOE**; supplement with contemporary techniques and local practice.
- **Anaesthesia for heart transplantation** — Edwards, Allen & Sidebotham, BJA Education 2021. Read for: recipient PVR, donor RV, graft reperfusion, separation and PGD (Chapter 13). [Open article](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.02.006)
- **[Pulmonary artery catheterisation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.08.003)** (BJA Education, 2024). **Useful for haemodynamic phenotyping** of LV versus RV failure and the limits of filling pressures; read selectively alongside the difficult-weaning chapter.
- **[BJA Education CABG Part 1, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.08.003)**
- **[BJA Education cardiac surgery-associated AKI, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.11.001)**
- **[BJA Education VV ECMO physiology, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.003)**

## ANZCA and Australasian sources

- **[ANZCA — Anaesthesia training program curriculum, Appendix Five](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/all-handbooks-and-curriculums/anzca-anaesthesia-training-program-curriculum.pdf).** Source of exact Final Examination learning outcomes; the workbook determines which components belong to Set 13.
- **[ANZCA — PG27(A), Guideline for major extracorporeal perfusion](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents).** Australasian professional framework for safe major extracorporeal perfusion. Local team protocols should operationalise the details.
- **[ANZCA — PG46, perioperative echocardiography (2025)](https://libguides.anzca.edu.au/anaestrain/ssu/cardiac).** Practice and competency standards for echocardiography use; relevant to diagnosis during difficult separation and ICU instability.
- **[Hegde S, Pearse B, Santifort K et al. Goal-directed bleeding management: understanding and implementing viscoelastic haemostatic assays across patient blood management](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1387).** Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) 2025, pages 59 onwards. Core source for applying ROTEM/TEG to actively bleeding patients and avoiding indiscriminate product administration.
- **[Johnstone L. The perioperative management of lung transplantation](https://airr.anzca.edu.au/anzcacrisjspui/bitstream/11055/1305/5/00_2025_Blue_Book.pdf).** Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) 2025. Relevant application of VA-ECMO/CPB versus off-pump support in non-cardiac/thoracic surgery; use as a clinical example, not as a universal transplant protocol.
- **[CALS-ANZ: Australasian ANZSCTS/ANZICS cardiothoracic advanced life support](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10692601/).** Source for cardiac surgical postoperative arrest management, pacing/shocks and the importance of trained early resternotomy.

## Blue Book reading alongside the question banks

- 2021: Khan and Scerri on post-bypass RV dysfunction, Falland and colleagues on RV failure, and Falland, Sidebotham and Allen on VADs for non-cardiac surgery. The ablation and vascular gas embolism chapters inform cath-lab complications. 2023: Emanuel on intravenous heparin informs anticoagulation and protamine alongside bypass-specific guidance. 2017: Winson and Brain on ECMO informs configuration and anaesthetic management. 2025: Hegde and colleagues on viscoelastic bleeding management, Chapman and Endlich on tracheal tumours, and Johnstone on lung transplantation.
- **[ANZCA Blue Book catalogue](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)**
- **[ANZCA Blue Book 2025](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305)**

## Current specialty guidelines

- **[2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP Guidelines on cardiopulmonary bypass in adult cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae354)** (published 2025). Primary modern reference for circuit, perfusion flow, temperature, cerebral/myocardial protection and CPB safety.
- **[2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP Guidelines on patient blood management](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae352)** (published 2025). Primary reference for transfusion, antifibrinolytics, haemostasis, protamine, VHA and postoperative bleeding.
- **[2024 EACTS Guidelines on perioperative medication in adult cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae355).** Relevant to preoperative antithrombotic decisions and postoperative resumption of therapy.
- **[ELSO guidelines and resources](https://www.elso.org/ecmo-resources/elso-ecmo-guidelines.aspx)**, including the 2021 adult VV respiratory failure guidance. Relevant to ECMO referral, patient selection, circuit and weaning; centres should use their latest approved protocols.
- **[2025 ERC Guidelines — special circumstances in resuscitation](https://www.resus.org.uk/professional-library/2025-resuscitation-guidelines/special-circumstances-guidelines).** Relevant to arrest in patients early after cardiac surgery, rapid shocks/pacing and expert resternotomy.
- **[2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/).** For current valve-treatment decisions and prosthesis context; the actual cardiac-surgery anaesthetic sequence is explained in Chapters 2–3.
- **[Australasian VV-ECMO clinical practice guideline (2026)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12955552/).** Australia/New Zealand GRADE guidance on selecting adults with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure; conditional recommendation and explicit assessment of longer-term neurological and functional outcomes.
- **Choudhury** — Post-cardiac transplant recipient: implications for anaesthesia (2017) — Denervation, reflex response, drug choices and perioperative organ/infection issues. [Source](https://doi.org/10.4103/ija.IJA_390_17)
- **ISHLT Guidelines for the Care of Heart Transplant Recipients (2023)** — Graft surveillance, immunosuppression, rejection and care around intercurrent surgery. [Source](https://www.ishlt.org/education-and-publications/standards-guidelines-detail/ishlt-guidelines-for-the-care-of-heart-transplant-recipients)
- **[2024 ERAS Cardiac/STS joint consensus](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.athoracsur.2023.12.006)**
- **[BJA Education 2026: Coronary artery bypass grafting, part 1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.08.003)**
- **[BJA Education 2026: cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.11.001)**
- **[BJA Education 2025: management of vasoplegic shock](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11785552/)**
- **[2026 Australasian VV-ECMO GRADE guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12955552/)**
- **[2026 Fifth Universal Definition of MI](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag101)**
- **[ANZCOR 11.10: CALS-ANZ](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-10-resuscitation-in-special-circumstances)**
- **[2026 review: Management of Shock After Cardiac Surgery](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42399040/)**
- **[ASH 2018 HIT management guideline](https://doi.org/10.1182/bloodadvances.2018024489)**
- **[ESC 2024 atrial fibrillation guideline](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehae176)**

## Authoritative textbooks for deeper reading

- **Kaplan’s Cardiac Anesthesia** — cardiopulmonary bypass, myocardial protection, difficult separation, cardiac surgical haemodynamics and TOE.
- **Miller’s Anesthesia** — cardiac anaesthesia and extracorporeal circulation sections, ventilation and postoperative critical care.
- **Cardiopulmonary Bypass: Principles and Practice (Gravlee et al.)** — fundamental perfusion science, pump/oxygenator physiology and myocardial protection.
- **Clinical Perfusion for Cardiac Surgery: A Step-by-Step Guide to the Fundamentals (Awad, DiNardo, Huang, Hancock; 2026)** — particularly useful for the perfusionist’s perspective and circuit troubleshooting.

## Oxford Handbook chapters and interventional-cardiology source reading

- **Freedman et al. Oxford Handbook of Anaesthesia, 5th ed.** Chapter 19 — Cardiac anaesthesia — [Open reference](https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780198853053.003.0019)
- 
- **Freedman et al. Oxford Handbook of Anaesthesia, 5th ed.** Chapter 34 — Anaesthesia for radiology and cardiology — [Open reference](https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780198853053.003.0034)
- 
- **Freedman et al. Oxford Handbook of Anaesthesia, 5th ed.** Chapter 5 — Cardiovascular disease — [Open reference](https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780198853053.003.0005)
- 
- **Freedman et al. Oxford Handbook of Anaesthesia, 5th ed.** Chapter 42 — Drug formulary — [Open reference](https://doi.org/10.1093/med/9780198853053.003.0042)
- 
- **Dooley N, Lowe M, Ashley EMC. Advances in electrophysiology and AF in the cardiac catheter laboratory, BJA Education (2018)** — [Open reference](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2018.08.001)
- 
- **EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS 2024 consensus on catheter and surgical AF ablation (including pulsed-field ablation)** — [Open reference](https://doi.org/10.1093/europace/euae043)
- 
- **2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease (TAVI and the Heart Team)** — [Open reference](https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines/Clinical-Practice-Guidelines/All-ESC-Practice-Guidelines/Valvular-Heart-Disease)
- 
- **2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI acute coronary syndromes guideline (PCI and radial access)** — [Open reference](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001309)
- 
- **2024 AHA/ACC perioperative cardiovascular guideline (CIEDs and perioperative device management)** — [Open reference](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.06.013)

## Redo cardiac surgery: supporting evidence


- **[Identifying patients at particular risk of injury during repeat sternotomy: analysis of 2555 cardiac reoperations](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtcvs.2010.07.086)** (Park et al., J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg, 2010). Injury rate, mortality with and without injury, and who is at higher risk.
- **[Reoperative cardiac surgery: challenges and outcomes](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3233317)** (Roselli, Tex Heart Inst J, 2011). Intraoperative adverse events, failure to rescue, imaging and tiered rescue strategies.
- **[Reoperative interval and perioperative mortality risk in cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamasurg.2024.5499)** (Ramsingh et al., JAMA Surgery, 2024). Contemporary resternotomy cohort: mortality by interval, transfusion, re-entry injury.
- **[Surgical factors and complications affecting hospital outcome in redo mitral surgery](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26984984/)** (Onorati et al., Eur J Cardiothorac Surg, 2016). Complication rates and predictors of death after redo mitral surgery.

items.title: PG27(A) (2015): Major extracorporeal perfusion
items.body:
**Source:** [ANZCA PG27(A): Guideline for major extracorporeal perfusion (2015)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/4a98f1fe-6af0-46ac-92d9-b00c94dad539/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/PG27%28A%29-Guideline-for-major-extracorporeal-perfusion-2015.PDF?language=en)

**Document status:** The 2015 guideline is listed on the ANZCA professional documents page; PG27/PG27BP are under review as of November 2026.

> **Core message:** Safe major extracorporeal perfusion (ECP) requires an organised service, appropriately qualified practitioners, a properly maintained heart–lung machine with functioning safeguards, explicit medical responsibility for prescriptions, validated checks, continuous monitoring, team communication and contingency plans.

> **How to read the wording:** This summary preserves the guideline's distinctions between **must**, **should**, and **recommended/ideal** requirements. It summarises the 2015 document, not additional contemporary CPB management guidelines.

## 1. Scope and responsibility

**Major ECP** diverts blood through an artificial circuit incorporating a **pump** to support the circulation and usually an **oxygenator** for O₂/CO₂ exchange. It is mainly used for cardiac/great-vessel surgery, but also for other forms of circulatory support.

### Service organisation

- ECP **should** be provided by an **organised, hospital-based service**, with sufficient trained personnel and resources for both routine and emergency work, including out-of-hours cover.
- The service **must have a designated head** accountable for administration and delivery.
- **Ideally**, the head is a registered medical practitioner. Otherwise, there **must** be an explicit reporting/accountability line to a registered medical practitioner (usually a cardiac anaesthetist or surgeon), who contributes to medication policies and takes medical responsibility for signing them off.
- The service must ensure equipment maintenance and stock records, regular review of ECP protocols with anaesthesia and surgical departments, and assessment of equipment effectiveness. Conducting relevant research is described as ideal.
- Dedicated facilities should accommodate hardware, appropriately protected disposable stock, **clean circuit-assembly space**, records/data and service administration, with access to the operating theatre and recovery/ICU.

### Clinical and prescribing accountability

- Major ECP **must only be managed by personnel with expertise in all aspects of the perfusion service**, including operating the heart–lung machine.
- If a **medical perfusionist** manages the case, that practitioner **must either operate the machine or directly supervise** its operation.
- **Prescribing drugs, complex solutions, fluids and blood products is a medical responsibility.** If the perfusionist cannot legally prescribe, there **must** be an explicit accountability line to a registered medical practitioner for **all drugs administered during ECP**.

**Exam distinction:** Technical operation of the bypass circuit and medical responsibility for medication prescription are separate duties; the guideline makes the accountability chain explicit.

## 2. Training and maintenance of competence

These are requirements for **medical practitioners undertaking independent responsibility for perfusion**; do not confuse them with the usual requirements for all anaesthetists participating in cardiac operations.

### Training: key numbers

| Requirement | PG27(A) recommendation |
|---|---|
| Entry qualification | Specialist-level physiology/pharmacology background (e.g. FANZCA); final-year advanced trainees may start if the relevant physiology/pharmacology components have been completed |
| Structured training | **At least 12 months, no more than 24 months** |
| Logbook | Required: circuit assemblies, actual perfusions, simulations and related activities |
| Total supervised-training experience | **At least 75 complete perfusions**, operating the heart–lung machine from start to end of bypass |
| First cases | **At least first 50** under **close supervision** by a fully trained medical perfusionist, including equipment assembly |
| Subsequent cases | May be undertaken independently **with a fully trained medical perfusionist immediately available** |
| Independent paediatric practice | The **same numerical requirements must be met specifically in paediatric cases** |

Training must also cover medical management on bypass (cardiovascular and gas-exchange parameters, acid–base, glucose/electrolytes, coagulation, blood conservation and blood products), as well as assembly and operation of the equipment. Relevant associated devices include cell salvage, haemofiltration, intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation, ECMO and familiarity with ventricular assist devices.

**Mandatory simulation competencies:**

1. **Main pump-head failure**.
2. **Gas entering the patient circuit**.
3. **Oxygenator changeout**.

Trainees **must demonstrate competence** in each to a fully trained medical perfusionist. The document also addresses recognition of practitioners trained before its promulgation, requiring appropriate capability/experience, current practice and hospital accreditation for their scope.

### Continuing professional development (CPD)

Ongoing relevant CPD is **required**, consistent with ANZCA CPD standards. The guideline provides these **recommended minimums** for medical perfusionists:

- Manage **at least 40 whole-body perfusions per year**, from initiation to cessation of bypass.
- **Personally operate** the heart–lung machine in **at least 20 of these cases**.
- Maintain a retrievable case record.
- Participate in continuing education, quality assurance, **periodic simulation** of the three critical scenarios above, routine audit of all patients and review of incidents.

**Exam numbers: 12–24 months | 75 perfusions | first 50 closely supervised | 40/year managed | 20/year operated.**

## 3. Heart–lung machine: essential equipment and safety safeguards

All electrical components should comply with relevant Australian/New Zealand standards for **cardiac-protected electrical safety**. The machine must meet applicable standards, undergo regular biomedical engineering inspection and maintenance, and have documented servicing and repair arrangements.

### Pump heads

- Console should generally have **three or more pump heads** capable of the required CPB flows (subject to clinical application).
- **Arterial pump**: alarms and servo-control (where appropriate), with manual override, for:
  - **Low reservoir blood level**.
  - **High arterial line pressure**.
  - **Bubble detection**.
- **All pump heads must** incorporate electronic **runaway protection**, be capable of straightforward calibration, display flow as **L/min or rpm**, and allow **manual emergency operation**.
- **An emergency hand crank must be immediately accessible.**
- Where a pump can reverse its direction, the reversal control must be lockable and require **two actions** to initiate reverse flow.
- Roller-pump heads require a **transparent removable cover** and an **adjustable occlusion mechanism**.

### Gas supply and oxygenation

- Connection to **indexed piped oxygen and air**, with appropriate alarms.
- A **readily available emergency oxygen supply** in case of piped-gas failure.
- Appropriate gas flowmeters and **gas blenders**.
- **Oxygen analyser must be used before and throughout CPB**, either in the gas supply to the oxygenator or the oxygenator's effluent gas.
- If volatile anaesthetics are administered via bypass, **waste-gas scavenging from the oxygenator is mandatory**.
- During CPB, oxygenator effluent gas **should** be continuously monitored for **O₂ and CO₂**, and for **volatile agent** if a vaporiser is fitted.

### Heat exchanger: numerical specifications

| Parameter | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Water temperature control | **4–42°C** |
| Water flow | **10–25 L/min** |
| Maximum water pressure | **600 mmHg** |
| Monitoring | Water-temperature monitoring, alarms and override; indications of pump failure and low water level |
| Backup | **A second heat exchanger must be available** |

The source may be an external hot/cold water system or a self-contained heater/cooler and pump. Water circulates through the exchanger in the oxygenator and/or blood reservoir.

### Monitoring and protection: know what is compulsory

| System | Required features / placement |
|---|---|
| **Reservoir low-level monitor** | **Must be used in every ECP**; audible and visual alarms plus servo-control of the primary blood pump, with override |
| **Arterial line pressure** | Measure outgoing circuit pressure towards the patient; line monitor at an appropriate point; pre- and post-membrane pressure **if possible** to measure transmembrane gradient; adjustable-pressure audible/visual alarms and pump servo-control with override |
| **Arterial gas-emboli detector** | **Macro-gas bubble detector must be used in every ECP**; arterial-line placement, audible/visual alarms and pump servo-control with override |
| **Venous haemoglobin O₂ saturation** | **Must be used during every CPB procedure**; sensor in venous return line at the point **most distal from the patient** to minimise streaming artefact; calibrate when applicable |
| **Blood temperature** | Arterial and venous blood temperature monitors, with adjustable audible/visual alarms |
| **Perfusionist's patient monitor** | Clearly visible ECG, intravascular pressures, core temperature and other relevant parameters |

Additional console equipment should include appropriate electrical/emergency power supplies, reservoir/oxygenator/tubing/filter attachments, reservoir illumination and suitable **cardioplegia delivery** equipment (pump, temperature control, bubble trap and pressure monitoring as needed).

**Exam distinction:** The document specifically makes **low-level detection and macro-gas-emboli detection mandatory for every ECP**, and **venous saturation monitoring mandatory for every CPB procedure**. It does not impose identical machine configurations on every non-CPB application.

### Disposable equipment and alternative ECP applications

- Disposable components **must** meet relevant manufacturing/quality standards, be checked for defects and **packaging/sterility breaches**, and be used with knowledge of manufacturer's instructions.
- Appropriate storage must protect stock against adverse environmental conditions.
- For other applications (e.g. acute cardiorespiratory support, transplantation or isolated organ/limb perfusion), machines should be **tailored to the application**, while relevant components should generally meet the heart–lung machine safety requirements.

## 4. Clinical management: before, during and after ECP

### A. Preoperative assessment

- Assess each patient for **ECP-specific requirements, additional risks and comorbidities** that may influence circuit or perfusion management.
- Discuss the planned perfusion and related services with the patient, **except when an emergency prevents this**.

### B. Before bypass: assembly and checking

- Circuit **must** be assembled, **checked and primed** according to **written institutional protocols**, respecting sterile handling, manufacturer instructions, choice of priming solution and a defined circuit check.
- Complete and **sign** an **electronic or written pre-bypass checklist** covering the assembled/primed circuit **and all machine components**; **retain the record**.
- **All medications added to the circuit must be checked and signed for** according to protocol.

### C. Starting ECP

- Perfusionist should be **immediately and exclusively available** for the patient and involved in perfusion management **from commencement of anaesthesia until chest closure** in cardiac surgery.
- Patient's **anticoagulation status must be assessed** for the intended procedure and **documented on the perfusion record**.

### D. Maintenance of ECP

- Continuously and vigilantly assess **physiological variables, coagulation and machine parameters**, with clearly displayed monitoring.
- Select **flow rates, perfusion pressures, gas exchange and acid–base strategy** using evidence where possible and **institutional protocols**.
- Account for comorbidities specifically identified by the guideline: **diabetes, renal/hepatic dysfunction, cerebrovascular disease and anaemia**.
- Maintain **clear, frequent communication between perfusionist, surgeon and anaesthetist**.

**Important:** PG27(A) requires individualised, protocol-based management but **does not provide a universal numerical CPB flow, MAP, ACT or temperature target**. Do not attribute such targets to this document.

### E. Weaning and cessation

- Weaning from ECP and re-establishing adequate **cardiac and respiratory function** require particular care and coordinated communication among the **perfusionist, anaesthetist and surgeon**.
- **The ECP circuit must remain functional** until **all three** agree it is no longer required.

**Exam pearl:** The guideline explicitly requires **joint agreement by surgeon + anaesthetist + perfusionist** before the circuit can cease to be maintained ready for use.

## 5. Emergency preparedness: protocols and drills

Basic ECP and anticoagulation protocols should be **evidence based**, jointly developed by perfusion/anaesthesia/surgery and regularly reviewed. Emergency protocols should be **distributed and regularly practised by all perfusion staff**.

Protocols **must address**:

1. **Gas leaks** or loss of gas supply.
2. **Blood-circuit leak or rupture**.
3. **Massive air embolism**.
4. **Pump failure**.
5. **Oxygenator malfunction**.
6. **Filter malfunction**.
7. **Heat-exchanger malfunction**.
8. **Clot detection in the circuit**.

**Remember the difference:** Three **training/CPD simulation scenarios** are **pump-head failure, gas in patient circuit, oxygenator changeout**; the **clinical emergency protocol** must cover the broader eight-scenario group above.

## 6. Perfusion record: mandatory content

A **contemporaneous electronic or written record must be made** and retained as part of the patient's medical record. It should document:

| Domain | Required detail |
|---|---|
| Case/patient | Patient identifiers, operation and relevant preoperative information |
| Personnel | Names of perfusion, anaesthetic and surgical staff |
| Hardware/disposables | Equipment and circuit details, including **serial numbers of major disposable components** |
| Safety checks | **Completed, signed pre-bypass checklist** |
| Monitoring | Monitored **machine** and **physiological** parameters |
| Medication and fluid | **All administered drugs/fluids**, including **composition of the prime** and subsequent additions |
| Myocardial protection | Cardioplegia **type, volume and route** |
| Balance/events | Fluid outputs and relevant intra-perfusion events |

Audit and incident review are also components of the service's ongoing quality-assurance programme.

## 7. High-yield numbers and mandatory safeguards — one-page review

| Topic | Memorise |
|---|---|
| Training duration | **12–24 months** |
| Training experience | **≥75 entire perfusions** |
| Close supervision | **First ≥50** cases, including assembly |
| Paediatric independent practice | **Same numbers in paediatric cases** |
| Suggested ongoing case volume | **≥40 managed/year**, including **≥20 machine-operated/year** |
| Pump heads | **≥3** generally |
| Heat exchange | **4–42°C; 10–25 L/min; ≤600 mmHg** |
| Backup heat exchanger | **Second unit available** |
| Emergency manual pump | **Accessible hand crank** |
| Reservoir safety | **Low-level detection in every ECP**, audible/visual alarm + servo-control |
| Air safety | **Macro-gas detector in every ECP**, audible/visual alarm + servo-control |
| Venous saturation | **Monitor in every CPB**; venous line, farthest from patient |
| Gas safety | **Backup O₂; oxygen analyser before/during CPB; scavenging if volatile used** |
| Before bypass | **Signed, retained checklist**; **checked and signed circuit drugs** |
| ECP end | Circuit ready **until surgeon, anaesthetist and perfusionist agree** |

## 8. Final Exam recall checklist

- Define **major ECP** and explain where it is used.
- Describe the **governance and medical prescribing accountability** required in an ECP service.
- State the **12–24 / 75 / 50** training numbers and the special **paediatric** rule.
- State the **40 / 20** recommended annual maintenance-of-practice numbers.
- Name the **three mandatory training simulation scenarios**.
- List the pump safety features: **runaway protection, low-level/high-pressure/bubble alarms, servo-control and hand crank**.
- Recall the **heat-exchanger temperature, water-flow and pressure specifications** and the required backup.
- State mandatory **O₂/gas supply, oxygen analysis and volatile scavenging** measures.
- Distinguish monitors required in **every ECP** from the venous saturation monitor required in **every CPB**.
- Describe the **venous saturation sensor position** and why the document specifies it.
- Describe the **pre-bypass checklist**, priming protocol and drug verification requirements.
- State the perfusionist's availability expectation and **anticoagulation documentation** requirement.
- Summarise the monitored variables, comorbidity considerations and **three-way communication** required on bypass.
- State who must agree before the **circuit can stop being kept functional**.
- Name the **eight categories of perfusion emergency** that local protocols must cover.
- List the essential elements of a **contemporaneous perfusion record**.

---

*Scope note: A structured summary of the **2015 ANZCA PG27(A)** guideline itself. It is not a replacement for local perfusion protocols, detailed cardiopulmonary bypass physiology/management guidance, or updated standards issued after 2015.*

items.title: 2026.2 Q9: Failure to wean from bypass after CABG
items.source: Past SAQ 2026.2 Q9 · no examiner's report yet
items.q: Describe your approach to the management of a patient who has failed to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) following coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).
items.model:
## Principle

A failed wean is a **diagnostic problem under time pressure**. Return to or stay on bypass, keep the heart decompressed and perfused, and work through a structured list rather than escalating inotropes blindly.

## 1. Check the basics (on bypass)

- **Rate and rhythm:** restore a rate and rhythm that support filling and output. Test epicardial sensing and capture, favour AV synchrony when possible, synchronise cardioversion for unstable organised tachyarrhythmia and defibrillate VF/pulseless VT.
- **Metabolic:** check adequate rewarming, potassium, magnesium, ionised calcium, pH and haemoglobin, and correct clinically important abnormalities.
- **Ventilation:** restore effective native ventilation, check gas exchange and lung expansion, and exclude tension pneumothorax.
- **Drug delivery:** confirm anaesthetic delivery and infusions, and review contributors to reduced contractility or vasodilation.

## 2. Find the cause: TOE, pressures and direct vision

**Do not accept a reassuring EF in place of a full haemodynamic diagnosis.** Inspect LV and RV cavity size, segmental function and LVOT VTI; distinguish a new graft-territory RWMA from global stunning. Review PA pressure, CVP, arterial waveform, pump-flow requirements, lactate and venous oxygen saturation. Air in coronary circulation may improve with de-airing and reperfusion time, whereas graft occlusion needs immediate surgical assessment or revision. After mitral surgery, dynamic SAM/LVOTO produces hypotension with a hyperdynamic rather than failing LV. Keep or return to full bypass until the reason for failure is defined and the patient is stabilised; repeated unsuccessful weans only increase myocardial injury.

| Cause | Clue | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **LV ischaemia** (graft kink or thrombosis, air in a coronary, poor protection) | Regional wall motion abnormality, ST change | Surgeon checks grafts and flows; revise or add a graft; GTN for spasm |
| **RV failure** (air in the right coronary, failed right grafting, protamine reaction, high PVR) | Dilated RV, septal flattening, rising CVP and reduced forward flow, new TR | See the sequence below |
| **Vasoplegia** | Good function, high output, low SVR, MAP below 65 | Titrate noradrenaline and consider vasopressin. Discuss rescue drugs for refractory vasodilation. |
| **Hypovolaemia, tamponade, valve dysfunction, dissection, LVOT obstruction** | Empty LV or TOE finding | Titrate volume if underfilled and treat per TOE or surgical findings |
| **Heart block** | ECG | Epicardial pacing |

## 3. Treat the haemodynamic cause

- **1.** **Preload and rhythm:** assess filling using TOE, measured flow and pressure trends. Titrate small pump-volume increments for genuine underfilling. Decompress an overloaded RV while maintaining AV synchrony and systemic perfusion.
- **2.** **Perfusion pressure:** support systemic and right coronary perfusion with titrated noradrenaline, adding low-dose vasopressin where appropriate.
- **3.** **Contractility:** choose dobutamine, adrenaline or milrinone according to ventricular function and arterial pressure. Pair vasodilating inotropes with pressure support as necessary.
- **4.** **RV afterload:** correct hypoxaemia, hypercarbia and acidaemia, recruit the lungs without overdistending them and consider inhaled nitric oxide or epoprostenol.

## 4. If still failing

- **Rest the heart:** return to full flow and retry.
- **IABP** may provide modest augmentation in selected patients but is not definitive support for severe isolated RV failure.
- **Mechanical support:** VA-ECMO, or an RVAD or LVAD; leave the chest open if swelling or bleeding prevents closure. VA-ECMO brings bleeding, limb ischaemia, stroke and differential hypoxia.

**Sources:** Official 2026.2 written paper, Q9. Examiner report not available in the checked Learn catalogue. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [BJA Education CABG Part 1 (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.08.003) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [BJA Education vasoplegic shock (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.10.004) · [BJA Education epicardial pacing (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10433321/)

items.title: 2026.1 Q7: Epicardial pacing in complete heart block before separation from bypass
items.q: A patient is in complete heart block prior to separation from cardiopulmonary bypass. a. Outline the programming considerations for epicardial pacing in this patient. (30%) b. Describe your approach to troubleshooting intermittent capture of the pacemaker in this patient who is pacing-dependent in the ICU. (70%)
items.model:
## a) Programming considerations

**Mode.** The patient is in complete heart block, so the ventricle must be paced. With atrial and ventricular wires and a sinus atrium, **DDD** (AV sequential) is best, because atrial systole contributes up to 25% of ventricular filling and AV sequential pacing generally improves ejection; AAI is relatively contraindicated in high-grade block. With ventricular wires only, or AF, use **VVI**. On weaning from bypass, an asynchronous mode (**DOO or VOO**) is acceptable while diathermy is in use and the chest is open, then change to a demand mode (DDD) afterwards, because asynchronous pacing risks R-on-T.

**Rate.** About **70 to 90 per minute**, chosen because the intrinsic rate is absent and a stunned, oedematous ventricle has a relatively fixed stroke volume so output is rate dependent; individualise to the output and ischaemia. **AV interval** 160 to 200 ms.

**Output.** Measure the **capture threshold** with experienced assistance, continuous ECG/arterial monitoring and effective backup pacing. In a dependent patient, do not deliberately provoke prolonged loss of capture to test the system. Under 5 mA is acceptable, 5 to 10 mA warrants discussion with the surgeon about new wires, over 10 mA is unacceptable. During supervised wire assessment/closure the surgeon may use a specific threshold-check protocol; the dependent ICU patient needs a reliable safety margin, commonly at least twice the measured capture threshold, with reassessment as thresholds change. **Sensitivity:** the sensing threshold can only be measured if there is an intrinsic rhythm, which a block may not allow; a dependent patient may need an asynchronous mode or close monitoring. Confirm mechanical capture on the arterial waveform.

## b) Intermittent capture in a pacing-dependent ICU patient

**Safety first.** Is the patient stable? If bradycardic or hypotensive, restore pacing immediately and use adrenaline or isoprenaline as a monitored bridge if required; atropine may be ineffective in complete/infranodal block and must not delay pacing, apply **transcutaneous pacing** pads, call for help, and start CPR if asystolic. Keep a defibrillator at the bedside.

**Systematic approach: patient, leads, generator.**

| Domain | Causes | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Patient** | Rising threshold (oedema, ischaemia, fibrosis; thresholds vary most in the first 48 hours), hypothermia (aim above 36 degrees), hypo or hyperkalaemia, acidosis, pericardial effusion or tamponade, drugs | Correct K, Mg, pH and temperature; echocardiogram; review drugs |
| **Leads** | Wire migration or fracture, loose connection at the wire, cable or box | Check from patient to box: wires at the skin, wire-to-cable, cable-to-box; replace the cable; try another wire or pole |
| **Generator** | Box off, flat battery, wrong mode, **output too close to threshold** so respiratory variation causes intermittent capture; oversensing (shivering, T waves, diathermy) inhibiting output; undersensing | Perform a full pacing check; raise output; reduce sensitivity setting for undersensing or raise it for oversensing; correct shivering; use an asynchronous mode if inhibited; change box and battery |

Intermittent pacing may also reflect a native escape rhythm competing with the paced rate: assess with experienced staff and a backup method; do not lower the rate or stop pacing unsafely in a dependent patient. Adjust the pacing rate only while preserving perfusion.

**Alternative modalities** if capture cannot be restored: transcutaneous pacing, a **transvenous wire**, or new epicardial wires; electrophysiology review, and a permanent pacemaker if block persists. If an R-on-T arrest occurs, pause the pacemaker, defibrillate, and follow cardiac surgical life support; do not leave a poorly sensing system running on a ward.

## Distinguish capture, sensing and output failure

**No pacing spikes** suggests inhibition/oversensing, cable/generator failure or an inappropriate rate/mode; **spikes without QRS** indicate failure to capture; **QRS without an arterial pulse** means absent effective mechanical output and requires resuscitation/diagnosis. Increase output promptly for capture failure while correcting causes. For oversensing, a higher numerical mV setting makes the box less sensitive; for undersensing, a lower mV setting makes it more sensitive. Do not assume every intermittent beat is a lead problem. Replace faulty equipment without interrupting effective pacing. Only measure a sensing threshold when intrinsic activity is present and doing so is safe.

DDD requires reliable atrial and ventricular sensing and is not automatically the safest mode with poor atrial sensing. Reassess rate and AV interval against arterial pressure, filling and ischaemia, rather than treating 70–90/min or 160–200 ms as universal prescriptions. Continue continuous monitored care, record mode/rate/output/sensitivity/thresholds and arrange specialist review before ICU discharge.

**Examiner linkage:** the 2026.1 report requires a justified mode/rate, a structured patient–leads–generator assessment, and alternative pacing to ensure safety; rate justification and rescue alternatives were common omissions.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.
rubric: **3 marks** — Justifies mode/rate/output/sensitivity/AV interval and confirms mechanical capture safely (part a)
**2 marks** — Stabilises the dependent patient and provides backup pacing
**3 marks** — Systematically assesses patient, leads and generator with capture versus sensing distinctions
**2 marks** — Corrects the fault and provides transcutaneous/transvenous/new epicardial alternatives and specialist follow-up

items.title: 2025.1 Q3: Discuss the perioperative management of an adult patient who underwent
items.q: Discuss the perioperative management of an adult patient who underwent heart transplantation three years ago and now requires an appendicectomy.
items.model:
## Preoperative assessment and preparation

Clarify appendicitis severity, perforation/sepsis, urgency, fasting/vomiting and need for source control. Contact the transplant team and review graft function, recent echo/ECG, functional capacity, rejection episodes, coronary allograft vasculopathy, arrhythmias and recent admissions. Absence of angina does not exclude graft ischaemia because cardiac afferents are denervated. Three years after transplant, opportunistic risk depends more on current immunosuppression/rejection therapy than on the date alone.

Review immunosuppressants and take an explicit plan for continuing them at the correct time, with an alternative route if oral absorption is unreliable. Tacrolimus/ciclosporin need attention to renal function, levels and CYP interactions; mycophenolate/azathioprine can cause cytopenia, and steroids cause diabetes/infection risk and possible adrenal suppression. Check FBC, renal/electrolytes (particularly potassium/magnesium), glucose and tests guided by illness. Do not independently stop anti-rejection drugs because surgery is urgent; severe sepsis may require a specialist-agreed modification. Continue usual steroid and provide stress supplementation when indicated by adrenal risk/stress.

Give effective appendicitis antibiotics guided by local flora, allergy and severity, with cultures if septic and no treatment delay. Use strict asepsis, quantify aspiration risk, consent to increased cardiovascular/infectious risk and plan postoperative monitoring. Resuscitation and source control proceed together; do not delay an urgent operation for every historic transplant record.

## Intraoperative management

The denervated heart has a higher resting rate, a reduced rapid reflex response to hypotension and a slower response to circulating catecholamines. Maintain adequate venous return, afterload and contractility; avoid abrupt vasodilatation, hypovolaemia, severe bradycardia and excessive fluid. Limited reinnervation can occur, so responses are not identical in every recipient.

For a stable patient with a full stomach, carefully titrated general anaesthesia with a cuffed tracheal tube is usually suitable; modify induction for shock and have direct-acting vasoactive drugs ready. Atropine and indirect sympathomimetics may be unreliable; use appropriate direct-acting agents and pacing if clinically needed rather than assuming routine prophylactic pacing. Monitor ECG, capnography, oxygenation and temperature; add an arterial line for significant sepsis/graft dysfunction/instability, not automatically solely for transplantation.

Laparoscopic pneumoperitoneum and position can reduce venous return, increase SVR and airway pressures, and alter CO2; ask for the lowest appropriate insufflation pressure, monitor tolerance, and agree conversion/desufflation if needed. Use protective ventilation and quantitative neuromuscular monitoring. Choose drugs with regard to organ function/interactions and avoid nephrotoxins. Preserve normothermia and glucose control.

## Postoperative management

Disposition reflects graft reserve, sepsis severity, surgery and haemodynamic support: monitored recovery may suffice for an uncomplicated stable case, whereas organ dysfunction/vasopressors require HDU/ICU. Ensure analgesia/antiemesis, early enteral drug delivery and documented immunosuppressant administration; monitor renal function, electrolytes, glucose, rhythm, infection and graft dysfunction. Communicate antibiotic and transplant-drug interactions with pharmacy. Involve the transplant team for an unexpected deterioration or missed anti-rejection doses.

The examiner specifically expected transplant physiology/pharmacodynamics, immunosuppressant management and postoperative care; an answer dominated by pacemakers misses the problem.

**Sources and review basis:** Official 2025.1 report, BT_PO 1.5; explicitly shared Master map. Blue Book 2019 cardiac-transplant chapter is background only unless read separately; current infection principles and transplant-team drug management inform the model. This is not an assertion that all cardiac-transplant questions belong to Set 4.
rubric: **2 marks** — Surgical urgency/sepsis and current graft/rejection/vasculopathy assessment.
**2 marks** — Specific continuation/route/interactions of immunosuppressants.
**2 marks** — Denervation and appropriate haemodynamic/drug implications.
**2 marks** — Anaesthetic/laparoscopic plan and appropriate monitoring.
**2 marks** — Postoperative disposition, organ/medication surveillance and handover.

items.title: 2022.1 Q8: IABP pressure trace at 1:2 augmentation
items.q: Identify the points labelled A to F on this intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) pressure-time trace at the commencement of 1:2 augmentation. (30%) Outline the aims of IABP placement and discuss the underlying physiological principles. (70%)
items.model:
## a) Identify A–F (30%)

The official report labels the trace as follows: **A** = unassisted systolic pressure (the original report prints “assisted systole/unassisted systole”); **B** = dicrotic notch, marking aortic valve closure; **C** = unassisted end-diastolic aortic pressure; **D** = diastolic augmentation (peak pressure after balloon inflation); **E** = assisted end-diastolic aortic pressure; **F** = assisted systolic pressure. In a 1:2 trace compare the unassisted and next assisted beats and describe the cardiac-cycle events, not merely whether peaks are higher or lower.

## b) Aims and physiological principles (70%)

The balloon lies in the descending thoracic aorta, just distal to the left subclavian artery, and is synchronised to the cardiac cycle. **Inflation immediately after aortic valve closure** displaces blood proximally and distally, creating an elevated aortic diastolic pressure. The proximal rise may increase coronary perfusion pressure and myocardial oxygen supply, particularly where coronary perfusion is pressure dependent. **Rapid deflation before the next systole** reduces aortic end-diastolic pressure and the pressure against which the LV ejects, reducing LV wall stress, stroke work and myocardial oxygen demand. These effects improve the myocardial oxygen supply–demand balance; any cardiac-output augmentation is modest and depends on underlying ventricular function.

Timing matters. **Early inflation** (before valve closure) opposes LV ejection, raising afterload. **Late inflation** loses part of diastolic augmentation. **Early deflation** forfeits sustained augmentation and may impair useful pressure support. **Late deflation** leaves an inflated balloon opposing LV ejection, raising assisted systolic pressure. Set 1:2 to compare waveforms and correct the inflation/deflation markers.

Performance depends on balloon size relative to aortic diameter, full balloon volume, correct position, reliable triggering, haemodynamic state and appropriate assist ratio. ECG triggering may be unreliable with arrhythmia, but arterial-pressure triggering can be used; a perfectly regular rhythm is **not** an absolute requirement. Consider IABP for selected ischaemic low-output states or inability to wean from CPB, remembering that it is not full circulatory support and does not provide a routine survival advantage in infarct-related cardiogenic shock. Avoid significant aortic regurgitation and aortic dissection; assess severe peripheral vascular disease, bleeding and vascular access risk.

**Examiner emphasis:** Candidates commonly used imprecise cardiac-cycle terminology, struggled to identify the dicrotic notch and confused increased diastolic coronary perfusion with systolic unloading. Link each named point to aortic valve opening/closure and LV pressure–volume work.

**Sources:** ANZCA 2022.1 Chair’s Report, p. 18. Pass rate 49.7%. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [IABP-SHOCK II](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1208410), [DanGer Shock](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2312572), and [ECLS-SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227)

items.title: 2020.2 Q1: Heart transplant recipient for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
items.q: You are asked to assess and anaesthetise a 54-year-old patient for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. They received a heart transplant ten years ago. Discuss the issues relevant for this patient.
items.model:
## Preoperative — graft, infection and organ reserve

Establish time since transplantation, rejection episodes, exercise tolerance, heart-failure symptoms and transplant follow-up. Examine current ECG, echocardiography, graft systolic/diastolic function, pulmonary pressure, known allograft vasculopathy and any prior coronary surveillance. **Cardiac allograft vasculopathy can present without typical angina** because sensory innervation is reduced; new fatigue, arrhythmia or LV impairment may indicate ischaemia or rejection. Look for renal dysfunction, hypertension, diabetes, infection and malignancy associated with long-term immunosuppression. Check FBC, electrolytes (especially potassium and magnesium), creatinine/eGFR and clinically indicated drug levels. Continue tacrolimus/ciclosporin, mycophenolate and corticosteroids as prescribed, arranging an alternative route if fasting; review drug interactions (macrolides, azoles, QT drugs), anaemia and infection prophylaxis. Discuss significant graft dysfunction or suspected rejection with transplant cardiology before elective surgery.

## Denervated cardiac physiology and drugs

The transplanted heart typically has a higher resting rate, diminished immediate reflex tachycardia with hypotension and a blunted chronotropic response to pain or hypovolaemia. Cardiac output is more dependent on venous return/stroke volume, especially with limited graft reserve; do not rely on heart-rate response to judge anaesthetic depth or volume status. **Direct-acting** agents (adrenaline, noradrenaline, phenylephrine and isoprenaline) act at adrenergic receptors; **indirect** agents such as ephedrine have variable efficacy. Atropine often has little chronotropic effect in a denervated heart (later reinnervation is variable). Have direct-acting chronotrope, pacing and defibrillation available. Any arrhythmia may have haemodynamic consequences, especially with CAV or rejection.

## Laparoscopy and intraoperative management

Pneumoperitoneum **reduces venous return**, can increase SVR and PVR, increases airway pressures and may cause hypercarbia; reverse Trendelenburg for upper abdominal surgery further reduces preload. These are specific risks that the 2020.2 examiners highlighted. Discuss a low insufflation pressure and gradual positioning, and be ready to release insufflation if output falls. Standard monitoring is reasonable with a stable graft but obtain an arterial line/TOE when disease or surgical risk warrants. Use carefully titrated induction, maintain intravascular volume without overload, avoid hypoxia/hypercarbia/acidosis and provide a safe airway/ventilation plan. Use meticulous asepsis and appropriate perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis. Do not give unnecessary nephrotoxic or interacting drugs.

## Postoperative

Resume immunosuppression promptly; monitor graft perfusion, renal function, glucose, infection and wound healing. Discuss the need for stress-dose steroids based on actual chronic steroid use/adrenal suppression, not transplant status alone. New hypotension, arrhythmia or reduced urine output should prompt usual surgical assessment and consideration of graft rejection, infection or silent ischaemia.

**Sources:** ANZCA 2020.2 Chair’s Report, p. 11. Pass rate 61.6%. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [ISHLT guidelines for the care of heart transplant recipients](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37080658/)

items.title: 2019.2 Q1: Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest: rationale and consequences
items.q: Describe the rationale for the use of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest and outline the pathophysiological consequences of this technique.
items.model:
## Rationale

**Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA)** stops the circulation completely at a core temperature of about 18 to 20 degrees Celsius, giving a **bloodless, cannula-free field** for aortic arch surgery, type A dissection, some thoracoabdominal and congenital operations and pulmonary thromboendarterectomy. The cost is ischaemia of every organ, and the aim is **cerebral protection**.

Cooling reduces the **cerebral metabolic rate** by about 6 to 7% per degree, to roughly 20 to 25% of normal at 18 degrees, and reduces excitatory neurotransmitter release and free-radical injury. An approximate 30–40-minute window for isolated arrest is often cited, but neurological risk is continuous and modified by adjunct antegrade cerebral perfusion; no fixed duration is guaranteed safe.

## Technique

**Cerebral perfusion is the variable that alters acceptable arrest duration.** Deep hypothermia in isolation does not guarantee a fixed duration without neurological injury: the operative anatomy, temperature attained, baseline cerebrovascular disease and use of selective antegrade cerebral perfusion all matter. In contemporary arch surgery, moderate hypothermia with antegrade cerebral perfusion is an accepted alternative to isolated DHCA. Track brain and body temperature at appropriate sites, arterial pressure and cerebral oximetry. Rewarm gradually and avoid cerebral hyperthermia. Confirm appropriate anticoagulation during cooling and plan haemostasis before rewarming; hypothermia-associated platelet dysfunction can persist after apparent temperature correction.

- Cool on bypass over 20 to 30 minutes, keeping the gradient between blood and body at 10 degrees or less; confirm brain cooling (nasopharyngeal and bladder or rectal temperature, EEG silence or cerebral oximetry).
- Adjuncts: head ice, steroids, a barbiturate or propofol, glucose control, an alpha-stat or pH-stat strategy (pH-stat favours cerebral blood flow during cooling), and **selective antegrade cerebral perfusion** or retrograde perfusion to extend the safe time.
- Rewarm slowly, keeping the outflow temperature below 37 degrees, to avoid gas emboli and cerebral hyperthermia.

## Pathophysiological consequences

| System | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Neurological** | Stroke, delirium, seizures, cognitive deficit, choreoathetosis in children; risk rises with arrest time |
| **Coagulation** | Platelet dysfunction, slowed enzyme activity, fibrinolysis, haemodilution and heparin: major bleeding |
| **Cardiac** | Bradycardia, VF below about 28 degrees, arrhythmias on rewarming, myocardial stunning |
| **Respiratory** | Left shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin curve, altered gas solubility and pH, lung injury |
| **Renal and visceral** | Ischaemia–reperfusion injury, acute kidney injury, gut ischaemia, cold diuresis |
| **Metabolic and inflammatory** | Hyperglycaemia (insulin resistance), acidosis, electrolyte shifts and a systemic inflammatory response that can lead to **vasoplegia** after rewarming |

Postoperatively expect prolonged ventilation, delayed awakening, bleeding and tamponade. DHCA is a distinct technique from cardioplegic arrest (a chemically arrested, perfused heart) and from ECMO (circulatory support).

**Updated reference:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline — hypothermia and cerebral protection](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/).

**Sources:** ANZCA 2019.2 report, Q1. Pass rate 44.3%. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [ACC/AHA aortic disease guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9876736/)

items.title: 2016.2 Q10: Considerations for successful weaning from bypass after CABG
items.q: Outline the considerations for successful weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass after coronary artery graft surgery.
items.model:
## Principle

Weaning is the **return of the native circulation and ventilation** once the heart and patient are ready. Prepare before the surgeon removes the clamp and complete a checklist.

## 1. Native circulation

**An ordered handover prevents missed mechanical causes.** Before asking the perfusionist to reduce flow, confirm graft patency and de-airing with the surgeon; use TOE for segmental and global function, ventricular filling, valve competence and unexpected LVOT obstruction. Each weaning attempt should identify which variable failed as pump support reduced—pressure, oxygen delivery, rhythm, ventricle or surgical anatomy. If the RV dilates while the LV empties, treat RV afterload/perfusion and consider coronary air. If the LV is hyperdynamic yet pressure remains low, assess low SVR or dynamic obstruction before choosing a drug.

- **Rate and rhythm:** aim for sinus rhythm or pacing at a rate titrated to filling and output. Use synchronised cardioversion for unstable organised tachyarrhythmia and defibrillation for VF. Test epicardial sensing and capture with backup available and use AV synchrony when appropriate. Correct important potassium and magnesium abnormalities.
- **Volume and MAP:** adequate preload by TOE and CVP; an individualised arterial pressure supported with a vasopressor when needed. Vasopressin can be relatively pulmonary-sparing at commonly used doses and may reduce catecholamine requirements; monitor PVR and clinical response. Vasoplegia is likelier with ACE inhibitors or ARB use, long bypass and poor ventricular function; milrinone worsens vasodilation.
- **Contractility and ischaemia:** good function on TOE, no new regional wall motion abnormality, graft flows checked.
- **De-airing** of the heart, vents off, cross-clamp off. Air in the anterior right coronary ostium is a classic cause of RV failure.
- **RV protection:** FiO2 1.0, no hypercarbia or acidosis, avoiding excessive tidal volume or PEEP; for patients with pulmonary hypertension or poor RV function start an inhaled pulmonary vasodilator (nitric oxide 10 to 20 ppm, up to 40) before bypass ends. Protamine can cause pulmonary hypertension, so give it slowly.

## 2. Native ventilation

Lungs **re-expanded** under vision (recruitment; check for pneumothorax or secretions), FiO2 1.0 and a working circuit before ventilation restarts.

## 3. Metabolic and haematological

- **Temperature** above 36 degrees (nasopharyngeal) with a small core-to-periphery gradient.
- **Acid-base, gases and electrolytes** normal; ionised calcium above 1.0.
- **Haemoglobin** adequate (about 70 to 80 g/L or above) and glucose controlled.
- **Coagulation:** Assess bleeding risk and prepare haemostatic testing. Once stable separation has been confirmed and the team agrees it is safe to reverse, titrate protamine and recheck anticoagulation and haemostasis.

## 4. Anaesthesia and equipment

Adequate depth and analgesia, transducers zeroed, TOE ready, defibrillator pads, and inotropes, vasopressors and vasodilators (GTN, nitric oxide) prepared.

## 5. The process

Communicate with the surgeon and perfusionist; wean gradually (partial then full clamping of the venous line) watching the heart, pressures and TOE; have a failure plan: reinstitute bypass, optimise preload, rate, contractility and afterload, then IABP or mechanical support.

**Sources:** ANZCA 2016.2 report, Q10. Pass rate 71.1%. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [BJA Education epicardial pacing (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10433321/)
