- **Trigger failure** with arrhythmia or pacing artefact: change to arterial pressure or internal trigger.
- **Gas leak** (blood in the tubing, alarms): stop and remove urgently, as the balloon can clot.
- **Position:** tip below the left subclavian (about 2 cm below the aortic knob).

## Complications

Limb ischaemia (the commonest), aortic injury or dissection, thrombocytopenia and haemolysis, infection, stroke or embolism, renal artery occlusion and gut ischaemia from migration, and bleeding.

## Weaning

Reduce the assist ratio from 1:1 to 1:2 to 1:3, or reduce augmentation, over hours, while monitoring pressures, urine output and lactate; remove when stable and anticoagulation allows, with firm pressure at the site and distal pulse checks. Avoid prolonged 1:3 ratio because of thrombosis.

## Practical points

Check the distal pulses, colour and temperature of both legs every hour while the balloon is in, and mark the area. A cold leg is an emergency: discuss removal or repositioning with the cardiologist at once, and give anticoagulation only as the team has agreed because it affects bleeding at the site.

**Sources:** ANZCA 2022.1 report Q8 · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes balloon mechanism and waveform
- Identifies timing errors (early and late inflation/deflation) and effects
- Other causes of poor augmentation (rhythm, volume, position, leak)
- Lists complications, especially limb ischaemia
- Actions for balloon rupture
- Describes weaning and removal

items.title: 22. Bypass and ECMO support for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: Outline the indications for cardiopulmonary bypass and ECMO in non-cardiac surgery and the anaesthetic issues of managing a patient on extracorporeal support.
items.a:
## Indications for bypass or ECMO support in non-cardiac surgery

- **Surgery on or near great vessels and the heart:** large thoracic or abdominal aortic aneurysm, tumours involving the vena cava or right atrium (renal cell carcinoma, thrombus), or pulmonary thromboendarterectomy.
- **Resection of airway or mediastinal masses** with expected airway loss: femoral veno-arterial or veno-venous ECMO before induction.
- **Pulmonary:** lung transplantation, tracheal resection, massive pulmonary embolism.
- **Cardiac or respiratory failure** needing support during an operation, and **hypothermic** or **drowning** rescue cases.
- **Trauma** (hepatic or caval injuries) and rarely **hyperthermia or poisoning** rescue.

## Planning

**Separate elective support from rescue and identify the exit.** For a large mediastinal mass or critical tracheal obstruction, discuss whether conventional airway rescue will be impossible and if pre-induction cannulation is warranted, with ECMO flow established in selected high-risk cases. The choice of VV versus VA support hinges on whether the anticipated failure is oxygenation alone or also cardiac output and systemic perfusion. Peripheral VA return can increase LV afterload and create differential upper-body hypoxaemia; right radial arterial gas and pulse oximetry may identify this. Establish who has authority for pump adjustment, emergency clamping, anticoagulation and circuit exchange, and confirm disposition to an appropriately staffed ICU. Rescue cannulation after profound collapse may be too late for safe induction.

Multidisciplinary meeting (surgeon, perfusionist, anaesthetist, intensivist), clear **indication and exit plan**, availability of a perfusionist and ECMO team, cannulation under local anaesthetic before induction where airway loss is a risk, and **heparin** with an ACT target (the 2017 chapter documents bleeding as the main complication, up to 79%). Platelets should exceed 100. Reversal strategy and rescue transfusion are planned.

## Circuit configurations (2017 chapter)

- **VV-ECMO:** oxygenation and CO2 removal; flow 3.5 to 6 L/min; oxygenation depends on ECMO flow relative to cardiac output; sweep gas controls CO2 (BJA 2024).
- **VA-ECMO:** circulatory and respiratory support; arterial pulsatility may be reduced; MAP reflects ECMO plus native flow and vascular resistance; risk of **differential hypoxia** (watch right-arm saturation) and LV distension.

## Anaesthetic issues

- Anticoagulation and bleeding; lung-protective ventilation (driving pressure below 15, plateau below 25); drug sequestration in the circuit (propofol, fentanyl), hypothermia and awareness monitoring.
- Positioning, line placement, and recognition of complications: air embolism, recirculation, access insufficiency, oxygenator failure.

Weaning is stepwise, with echocardiography to confirm recovery, and reversal of heparin avoided in the circuit.

## Practical points

Agree in advance who is responsible for the circuit during induction and transport, and keep a clamp and a hand crank available. Check that anaesthetic drug delivery is by TIVA or through the oxygenator exhaust, and record the ACT and the flows at fixed intervals, because small changes can cause large haemodynamic effects.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book 2017, ECMO anaesthetic perspectives](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [Blue Book 2025, airway obstruction and thoracic support chapters](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [BJA Education VV ECMO (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.01.001)

## Self-marking checklist

- Lists CPB indications in non-cardiac surgery
- Lists ECMO indications (airway, transplant, PE, cardiac arrest)
- Describes VV versus VA configurations
- Plans team, cannulation timing and anticoagulation
- Monitoring including differential hypoxia and pre- and post-oxygenator saturations
- TIVA and depth of anaesthesia
- Complications and contraindications

items.title: 23. ECMO for severe respiratory failure
items.q: Outline the indications for ECMO in severe respiratory failure and the principles of its delivery.
items.a:
## Principle

VV ECMO drains venous blood, oxygenates it across a membrane and returns it to the venous circulation. It provides gas exchange and permits less injurious ventilation. Oxygenation depends on effective circuit flow relative to cardiac output, recirculation, native-lung function, membrane gas oxygen fraction and haemoglobin. Sweep mainly controls CO₂ clearance. Correcting hypoxaemia and hypercapnia may also improve RV afterload.

## Indications

Refer early for severe, potentially reversible respiratory failure after optimising protective ventilation and prone positioning when suitable. A PaO₂/FiO₂ below 80 mmHg or severe persistent hypercapnic acidosis (pH below 7.25 with PaCO₂ at least 60 mmHg despite optimal settings) are examples of triggers for specialist assessment. Selection considers severity, trajectory, reversibility and a viable bridge, including transplant when appropriate.

**Evidence:** CESAR (180 patients; survival without disability at 6 months 63% versus 47%, confounded by transfer to a specialist centre and protective ventilation); EOLIA (249 patients; no significant 60-day mortality difference, but 28% of controls crossed over); meta-analyses showed RR for death 0.73 at 60 days. Survival in the 2015 ELSO registry for VV was 57%.

## Contraindications

An irreversible process without a viable decannulation or transplant plan generally precludes VV ECMO. Major neurological injury, bleeding or anticoagulation limitations, longer exposure to injurious ventilation, frailty and multiorgan failure require individual specialist assessment.

## Management on ECMO

**Troubleshoot low oxygenation as a circuit–patient interaction.** Adequate post-oxygenator PaO₂ with persistently low patient saturation suggests recirculation, high native cardiac output relative to circuit flow, cannula malposition or residual lung shunt. Increasing sweep mainly improves CO₂ clearance; it does not reliably correct severe hypoxaemia if ECMO blood flow is inadequate. Signs of access insufficiency include chattering, very negative drainage pressure and reduced flow despite higher RPM; evaluate preload, position, cannula position and obstruction rather than simply driving the pump faster. Monitor pressure gradients, haemolysis, fibrin deposition and circuit oxygen transfer. The patient's physiology and ELSO criteria determine timing and candidacy rather than a single P/F ratio in isolation.

- **Ultraprotective ventilation:** driving pressure below 15, plateau below 25, rate 4 to 15, tidal volume below 4 mL/kg, to rest the lung.
- **Anticoagulation** with heparin; bleeding (5 to 79%) is the main complication, so set bleeding and anticoagulation thresholds by indication and local ECMO protocol; a fixed platelet target is not universal and check the circuit.
- Complications: **recirculation** (cannula tips 10 to 15 cm apart), access insufficiency, air embolism, oxygenator failure, infection up to 45%, and haemolysis.
- Drug sequestration in the circuit (lipophilic drugs).

## Weaning

As native-lung gas exchange recovers, reduce delivered oxygen and sweep under unit protocol and assess an off-sweep trial using adequate circuit blood flow. Confirm acceptable oxygenation, pH, CO₂ and work of breathing on safe ventilator support before decannulation.

**Sources:** [BJA Education VV ECMO (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.01.001) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2017, ECMO anaesthetic perspectives](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains early referral, oxygenation and hypercapnic criteria, reversibility and bridge options
- Cites CESAR/EOLIA and the referral model
- Lists contraindications
- Describes the circuit and cannulation
- Explains oxygenation versus CO2 clearance
- Anticoagulation and lung-protective ventilation
- Complications and weaning

items.title: 24. Hypoxaemia on VV ECMO
items.q: A patient on VV ECMO becomes hypoxaemic. Explain your assessment, how to distinguish membrane failure from other causes, and how to calculate membrane oxygen transfer.
items.a:
## Assess patient and support together

Call the ECMO team, confirm a reliable saturation/arterial sample, assess perfusion, Hb, lactate, temperature and respiratory/circulatory state. Give appropriate native-lung oxygen/ventilatory rescue while protecting the lung. Inspect gas supply, blender delivered O2 fraction, sweep tubing, pump power/settings, measured blood flow, circuit/cannula integrity and alarms. A normal RPM does not prove normal flow.

**Oxygenation** depends strongly on effective ECMO flow relative to cardiac output, Hb/oxygen content, recirculation, membrane function and residual lung gas exchange. Sepsis/fever or agitation can raise CO and oxygen consumption so a previously adequate flow becomes inadequate. Treat the precipitant and optimise safe flow; indiscriminate beta-blockade to raise saturation can reduce oxygen delivery. **Sweep flow** primarily changes CO2 clearance, whereas delivered gas oxygen fraction is a separate oxygenation setting. Turning up sweep alone does not correct every desaturation.

## Drainage and recirculation

Check for kink/migration, IVC collapse, high intrathoracic/intra-abdominal pressure, tamponade or true hypovolaemia. Chatter/negative drainage pressure may worsen when RPM is increased. Reduce excessive suction under specialist control and correct the cause; fluid is appropriate only when underfilling is demonstrated. Recirculation returns oxygenated blood directly to drainage instead of systemic delivery. Check cannula positions and dual-lumen return-jet direction with imaging; adjust configuration/position with the ECMO team. High drainage saturation may reflect recirculation but can also reflect altered systemic extraction; integrate findings.

## Membrane assessment

Compare pre/post-membrane gases at known blood flow and delivered oxygen fraction, pressure-gradient/resistance trends, visible thrombus, haemolysis, falling platelets/fibrinogen and rising D-dimer. Falling post-membrane oxygen tension/content, poor CO2 removal or increasing resistance suggests dysfunction; exclude gas-supply/condensation problems first. The 2026 review cites post-membrane PaO2 <25 kPa or a >50% decline at FdO2 1.0 and low oxygen transfer as warning features, not stand-alone universal exchange rules. Pressure gradient is flow- and device-dependent: compare resistance/trends rather than a fixed pressure alone. Prepare a planned trained membrane/circuit exchange when indicated before sudden failure.

## Worked calculation

With Hb **9 g/dL**, pre-membrane saturation **65%**, PO2 **5 kPa**, post-membrane saturation **100%**, PO2 **40 kPa**, and flow **4 L/min**:

- Oxygen content (mL/dL) = **1.34 × Hb × saturation fraction + 0.023 × PO2(kPa)**.
- Pre-membrane content = 1.34×9×0.65 + 0.023×5 = **7.95 mL/dL**.
- Post-membrane content = 1.34×9×1.00 + 0.023×40 = **12.98 mL/dL**.
- Transfer = 4 L/min × (12.98−7.95) mL/dL × 10 dL/L = **approximately 201 mL O2/min**.

This measures oxygen added by the membrane, not total systemic oxygen delivery or proof the patient has adequate oxygenation. A low value may reflect low flow or high inlet saturation as well as membrane failure. Evaluate it in context and avoid rapid large CO2 changes during support adjustments.

**Sources:** [BJA Education VV ECMO physiology (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534926000296) · [BJA Education VV ECMO (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.01.001) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2017, ECMO anaesthetic perspectives](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Assesses patient/perfusion and verifies actual circuit/gas function
- **2 marks** — Explains flow/CO/Hb/consumption versus sweep physiology
- **2 marks** — Distinguishes drainage failure and recirculation
- **2 marks** — Uses gases/resistance/haemolysis trends to assess membrane function
- **2 marks** — Calculates content difference × flow with correct units and limitations

items.title: 25. Complications in the first 24 hours after cardiac surgery
items.q: Outline the common complications in the first 24 hours after cardiac surgery and their management.
items.a:
## Approach

Deterioration after cardiac surgery is approached systematically: **A, B, C** then **C** for the circulation, using the causes of low cardiac output.

## Circulation (commonest)

**Distinguish three time-critical patterns.** Persistent high drain loss with hypotension suggests ongoing surgical haemorrhage or acquired coagulopathy; suddenly diminished drain output with rising filling pressures and falling cardiac output may indicate an obstructed drain and localised tamponade, despite apparently little blood loss. A new regional wall-motion abnormality or malignant arrhythmia raises concern for graft occlusion, air embolism or perioperative infarction; notify the surgeon urgently for possible reintervention. Low MAP with preserved LVOT VTI and a warm circulation points toward vasoplegia after excluding mechanical causes. Use serial lactate, capillary refill, urine output, SvO₂ and bedside echo together rather than treating MAP alone. Document when the surgeon was called and set explicit thresholds for escalation.

- **Bleeding and tamponade:** drain output above about 200 mL/h or suddenly stopping drains, rising CVP and falling pressure with equalised diastolic pressures. Tamponade can be localised and missed on TTE (use TOE). Treat coagulopathy and return to theatre; in arrest, resternotomy within five minutes.
- **Pump failure:** LV from graft failure or perioperative infarct; **RV failure** (see R02); valve or prosthesis problem. Use ECG, troponin, echo.
- **Vasoplegia**, hypovolaemia.
- **Arrhythmia:** AF occurs in 10 to 40% after CABG, 37 to 50% after valve and up to 70% after combined surgery, peaking at about 48 hours. Rate control first when stable; synchronised DC cardioversion if unstable; K, Mg, beta-blocker continuation and amiodarone for prevention. Heart block is common after valve surgery (mitral 23.5%, aortic 10.3%); epicardial pacing.

## Other systems

- **Respiratory:** atelectasis, pneumothorax, phrenic injury, pleural effusion, ARDS.
- **Neurological:** stroke, delirium, cognitive change.
- **Renal:** AKI.
- **Gastrointestinal and metabolic:** gut ischaemia, hyperglycaemia, lactate.
- **Infection:** sternal wound infection and mediastinitis.

## Immediate management

Reassess, monitor with arterial line and CVP, **12-lead ECG, chest X-ray, ABG and lactate**, and TOE for tamponade, ventricular function and valves. Correct electrolytes, ventilate, treat the cause, and communicate with the surgeon early.

## Cardiac arrest

Use CALS-ANZ for a monitored arrest after cardiac surgery. Witnessed VF/pulseless VT may receive up to three immediately available stacked shocks. Pace severe bradycardia or asystole when epicardial wires are available. Start compressions if those immediate manoeuvres fail to restore circulation within 60 seconds and continue while the skilled team prepares resternotomy, aiming to reopen within five minutes.

## Practical points

Hand over the operation, the grafts, the lines and drains, and the specific concerns of the surgeon to the ICU team, and agree thresholds for calling the surgeon, such as drain output above 200 mL per hour or a falling cardiac index. Review the first chest X-ray for line position and pneumothorax, and keep pacing wires connected to a working box in the first 48 hours.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [BJA Education epicardial pacing (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10433321/) · [BJA Education perioperative AF (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.10.006) · [ANZCOR 11.10, CALS-ANZ](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-10-resuscitation-in-special-circumstances)

## Self-marking checklist

- Low cardiac output with causes and TOE assessment
- Tamponade recognition and resternotomy
- Arrhythmias (AF) and management
- Bleeding: causes, coagulation testing and treatment
- Respiratory complications
- AKI and neurological complications
- Multimodal analgesia and ICU care

items.title: 26. Early graft failure after CABG
items.q: Three hours after initially uncomplicated CABG, a sedated patient develops hypotension, new inferior ST elevation and a new inferior regional wall-motion abnormality. Outline how you would assess and manage suspected early graft failure.
items.a:
## Recognise suspected graft failure

Treat the combination of new territorial ST elevation, regional dysfunction and shock after an initially stable period as possible acute coronary compromise. Postoperative repolarisation changes and troponin release are common, but a new wall-motion abnormality in the corresponding graft territory and deteriorating perfusion make this time-critical. Inform the cardiac surgeon, interventional cardiologist and ICU team immediately. Review which territories were grafted, intraoperative flow measurements, the separation TOE, intraoperative ECG and the exact timing of deterioration.

## Stabilise while investigating

Confirm the arterial waveform and obtain a 12-lead ECG compared with baseline. Support oxygenation and ventilation, treat significant rhythm disturbances, and titrate noradrenaline or inotropy to coronary and systemic perfusion while arranging definitive assessment. Assess blood loss, drain patency, Hb, lactate, acid–base status, potassium and ionised calcium. Obtain urgent echocardiography, using TOE if transthoracic views are inadequate. Compare regional with global LV function and assess the RV, filling, valves and the pericardium. Look for tamponade from localised clot, major haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, severe vasoplegia or another cause of the shock. A regional abnormality can occur with stunning, and the absence of a diagnostic ECG pattern does not exclude graft compromise.

## Identify the mechanism and confirm the diagnosis

Consider acute graft thrombosis, kinking or anastomotic obstruction, conduit spasm, incomplete revascularisation and new native coronary occlusion. Other causes include coronary air and inadequate myocardial protection. Request serial troponin and evaluate change from the preprocedural result when available. The 2026 universal definition distinguishes expected procedural myocardial injury from infarction caused by a coronary complication. It integrates clinical deterioration or ischaemic features with serial biomarkers and imaging. Higher or persistently rising values strengthen concern, but a threshold alone cannot establish the diagnosis. Do not wait for a later troponin result before acting on shock with strong clinical evidence of coronary compromise.

## Restore perfusion and plan follow-up

Arrange urgent angiography if severe ischaemia or graft failure is suspected and transfer is feasible. Angiography can distinguish graft and native-vessel pathology and enable PCI. Involve both teams in choosing native or graft PCI, surgical graft revision or re-exploration based on anatomy, timing, concurrent bleeding, need for other surgical repair and the patient’s stability. A surgical emergency such as tamponade or uncontrollable bleeding may require immediate reopening instead. Coordinate antithrombotic therapy with the procedural team because early postoperative bleeding and stent requirements compete. If shock persists, agree temporary support and an exit strategy. After reperfusion, reassess mechanics, ECG, lactate and organ perfusion, and hand over the antiplatelet and surveillance plan.

**Sources:** [BJA Education CABG Part 1 (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.08.003) · [2026 Universal Definition of MI](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13523810/) · [EACTS consensus on perioperative MI](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezad415)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises the graft-territory pattern and activates the surgeon and interventional team early
- Stabilises perfusion and excludes tamponade, bleeding and other causes in parallel
- Compares ECG and echo with baseline and names graft and native-coronary causes
- Interprets serial troponin and imaging without delaying intervention for biomarker criteria
- Plans urgent angiography or reopening and weighs PCI versus graft revision
- Coordinates antithrombotic decisions, temporary support and post-reperfusion surveillance

items.title: 27. Acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery
items.q: Discuss the pathophysiology, risk factors and prevention of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery.
items.a:
## Importance

AKI affects up to 30% of patients after cardiac surgery, and dialysis-requiring AKI carries a high mortality. It is also a feature of VAD surgery (AKI 18 to 43.5% in non-cardiac surgery) and vasoplegia.

## Pathophysiology

- **Ischaemia-reperfusion injury** and low flow on bypass: non-pulsatile flow and a perfusion pressure below the renal autoregulatory limit, with the kidney's medulla borderline for oxygen.
- **Inflammation** (SIRS), complement activation and **haemolysis**: free haemoglobin and iron, with cell salvage and prolonged pump time worsening this.
- **Microemboli, atheroma and nephrotoxins** (contrast, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, vancomycin).
- **Low cardiac output, vasoplegia, high-dose vasoconstrictors and venous congestion.**
- **Transfusion**, anaemia and hyperthermia on rewarming.

## Risk factors

Preexisting CKD, diabetes, age, heart failure and low EF, emergency or redo surgery, combined procedures, long bypass and cross-clamp times, preoperative ACE inhibitor or diuretic, anaemia, and peripheral vascular disease.

## Prevention (bundle)

**Current prevention is more nuanced than raising MAP with vasopressors.** The 2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guidelines recommend against routinely targeting a high MAP using vasoconstrictors solely to prevent AKI. Focus on adequate oxygen delivery (pump flow × arterial oxygen content), avoiding haemodilution, anaemia, prolonged hypotension and venous congestion. A personalised perfusion goal should consider baseline blood pressure and metabolic indicators, not a single prophylactic MAP. The same guidelines say perioperative balanced amino-acid infusion may be considered to reduce AKI, whereas prophylactic diuretics and low-dose dopamine should not be portrayed as renoprotective. Diagnosis uses KDIGO creatinine and urine-output changes; transient oliguria during bypass requires contextual assessment rather than automatic fluid boluses.

- Preoperative: delay surgery after contrast if possible; stop nephrotoxins.
- **Perfusion:** maintain adequate pump flow and systemic oxygen delivery, avoid excessive haemodilution and assess MAP in physiological context; routine high vasopressor-driven MAP targets have not prevented AKI in trials (2024 CPB guideline).
- Minimise bypass time, consider off-pump surgery, avoid haemolysis and suction.
- Avoid hypotension, vasoconstrictor overuse, hyperglycaemia and hypovolaemia; use goal-directed haemodynamics and balanced crystalloid.
- Treat cause of low output; avoid nephrotoxins. No drug (dopamine, fenoldopam, furosemide, mannitol, bicarbonate) is proven protective.

## Management of established AKI

Define with KDIGO stage (creatinine rise or urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h). Optimise volume and perfusion, remove nephrotoxins, correct hyperkalaemia and acidosis, adjust drug doses, and start renal replacement for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemia; timing of early versus delayed RRT remains debated.

## Practical points

Record a baseline creatinine before surgery and check it daily for the first three days, because the rise often appears after 24 to 48 hours. Avoid nephrotoxic combinations in the first week, and adjust drug doses in anyone whose urine output falls. Early discussion with nephrology is sensible for stage 2 or 3 AKI.

**Contemporary CPB reference:** [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP 2024 guidelines](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/).

**Sources:** [BJA Education cardiac surgery-associated AKI (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.11.001) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines CSA-AKI (KDIGO) and its burden
- Lists the mechanisms (ischaemia–reperfusion, haemolysis, inflammation)
- Lists patient and operative risk factors
- Describes preventive care (perfusion pressure, nephrotoxin avoidance, KDIGO bundle)
- Notes interventions without benefit
- Describes management and renal replacement indications

items.title: 28. Ventricular fibrillation in ICU after cardiac surgery
items.q: A patient fibrillates in the ICU four hours after cardiac surgery. Describe the management, including the role of internal defibrillation.
items.a:
## Context

After cardiac surgery, an arrest is usually VF/pulseless VT, asystole or pacing failure, and **tamponade, bleeding, tension pneumothorax, hypovolaemia and graft occlusion** are common causes. The management follows **cardiac surgical life support** rather than standard ALS, because external compressions are less effective and may injure the heart or sternal repair.

## Rhythm-specific approach

**Use the current Australasian protocol precisely.** ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 (September 2026) endorses CALS-ANZ after cardiac surgery: for witnessed monitored VF/pulseless VT with immediately available defibrillation, attempt up to three promptly delivered stacked shocks; severe bradycardia/asystole with epicardial wires may be treated with emergency DOO pacing; if the patient is paced in PEA, briefly pause pacing to exclude concealed VF. External compressions may be withheld for up to 60 seconds for these immediate manoeuvres, but should then start if there is no ROSC and must continue while emergency resternotomy is prepared. Aim for resternotomy by a skilled team within five minutes. Seek tamponade, blood loss, ischaemia, tension pneumothorax and pacing failure from the outset.

- **VF/pulseless VT:** if witnessed and monitored with a defibrillator immediately available, give up to three stacked shocks. If unsuccessful, continue resuscitation and prepare to reopen.
- **Asystole/bradycardia:** check connections and use emergency asynchronous DOO pacing with atrial and ventricular wires available. Verify mechanical capture and start compressions when initial manoeuvres fail.
- **PEA:** in a paced patient, briefly pause pacing to exclude hidden VF. Initiate compressions promptly and treat reversible causes.
- Avoid **adrenaline** boluses initially (risk of rebound hypertension and bleeding); use amiodarone 300 mg after the third failed shock.

## Defibrillation

Use biphasic external energy appropriate to the defibrillator and local guidance. With an open chest use internal paddles, commonly 20 J per CALS-ANZ, and ensure contact and team clearance. If an ICD is in situ, the device should be left or magnet applied only per plan.

## Resternotomy

Do **emergency resternotomy within five minutes** if shocks fail, or if the cause is tamponade. Prepare a pack, ensure the surgeon, perfusionist and scrub nurse call; internal massage is more effective than external; consider rapid return to bypass or ECMO (extracorporeal CPR).

## Anaesthetic role

Airway and ventilation with 100% oxygen, treat reversible causes (volume, K, Mg, calcium, pH, tension pneumothorax), drugs and fluids via central access, TOE for tamponade, and avoid vasopressin or calcium unless indicated. Record the time of arrest.

## Post-arrest

Recovery in ICU with post-arrest care and temperature control as indicated, evaluation of cause (echo, ECG, graft assessment), neurological monitoring, and an early plan for mechanical circulatory support if unstable.

## Practical points

Practise the sequence in a simulation with the whole ICU team, because the time to resternotomy depends on rehearsal and a clear call. Keep the resternotomy set at the bedside, and know where the nearest sterile gown and gloves are. After any event, report it and debrief the team.

**Sources:** [ANZCOR 11.10, CALS-ANZ](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-10-resuscitation-in-special-circumstances) · [BJA Education epicardial pacing (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10433321/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises arrest causes specific to cardiac surgery
- Gives up to three shocks first, then CPR and resternotomy
- Notes adrenaline and amiodarone modifications
- Pacing for asystole or bradycardia with wires
- Emergency resternotomy within 5 minutes
- Describes internal paddles and typical initial energy of 20 J
- Treats reversible causes

items.title: 29. Polymorphic VT with epicardial wires in DDD mode
items.q: A patient with temporary epicardial wires develops recurrent polymorphic VT despite a normal QT. The pacing box is in DDD mode and pacing spikes appear near T waves. Explain the mechanism and your management.
items.a:
### Recognise a pacing-induced arrhythmia

Assess pulse and circulation immediately. Sustained unstable polymorphic VT or VF requires **unsynchronised defibrillation** and the applicable resuscitation pathway; do not wait for synchronisation or a full device analysis. Ask for cardiac surgery/ICU and EP assistance and review saved telemetry without delaying rescue. Stop the pacing system from continuing to trigger unsafe impulses while providing resuscitation and a reliable alternative if the patient is dependent. Simply turning off all pacing and leaving a dependent patient unsupported is unsafe.

### Why a demand mode can still produce R-on-T

Demand pacing is safe only when intrinsic signals are sensed reliably. **Undersensing** may result from poor wire signal, migration, cable/connection problems or a sensitivity value set too high. Inappropriate impulses can then fall during ventricular repolarisation and trigger polymorphic VT/VF. Normal QT does not exclude this mechanism and does not make the rhythm torsades de pointes.

In DDD pacing, poor **atrial** sensing can also provoke ventricular R-on-T. An unsensed intrinsic P wave may be followed by an inappropriate atrial impulse overlapping a conducted ventricular beat. Ventricular blanking after that atrial impulse can conceal the true R wave; the box subsequently emits a ventricular impulse after its programmed AV interval, potentially onto the T wave. Thus the atrial circuit and timing need review, not only the ventricular output. Higher output does not repair an inability to sense intrinsic activity.

### Restore a safe system

Review dependence, underlying atrial/ventricular rhythm and perfusion. Check the patient, wires, connections and generator systematically; correct hypothermia, hypoxia, K/Mg/Ca abnormalities, acidosis and ischaemia. Confirm settings and inspect for oversensing, crosstalk, tracking of AF/flutter or pacemaker-mediated re-entry. These mechanisms need different solutions.

With expert staff and immediate rescue available, establish sensing and capture thresholds when safe. **Lower mV setting means greater sensitivity**; set an appropriate margin below the measured intrinsic signal without producing noise oversensing. If no intrinsic rhythm exists, routine sensing measurement is not possible. If the patient does not need pacing, leaving an unreliable backup system switched on can add danger: an expert may turn it off and continue observation. If dependent, use a reliably functioning simpler mode/wire system or urgent transvenous/new epicardial support, maintaining intensive monitoring. Asynchronous mode is a supervised emergency option when necessary, not routine ward backup.

### Prevent recurrence and identify complications

Verify electrical and mechanical capture and monitor continuously after any change. A low rate setting is not inherently safe in an inadequately sensing DDD system. Document thresholds, settings, dependence, rationale and backup plan, checking at least daily and after major clinical changes. Do not transfer a patient with unreliable sensing to an unmonitored ward.

The same safety review includes wire removal: coordinate pacing need, coagulation/antithrombotics and local removal policy. Resistance requires stopping and surgical advice. New shock after removal needs urgent echo for tamponade; the observation plan must continue after the wire is out. Evidence is largely practical/observational, but the mechanisms and preventable hazards are directly relevant to external pacemaker programming outcomes. [TEMP][TEMP]

## Self-marking checklist
- Treats sustained polymorphic VT/VF immediately
- Identifies R-on-T from undersensing rather than assuming long-QT torsades
- Explains the atrial-sensing/ventricular-blanking DDD mechanism
- Protects pacing-dependent patients during system interruption
- Distinguishes output from sensing and lower mV from greater numerical sensitivity
- Uses a systematic patient–wire–generator check and a reliable alternative
- Avoids unsafe ward backup and documents daily checks
- Recognises wire-removal tamponade and plans surveillance

items.title: 30. Duration of ventilation and fast-track after cardiac surgery
items.q: Discuss the factors that influence the duration of postoperative ventilation after cardiac surgery and the role of fast-track management.
items.a:
## Concept

**Fast-track** cardiac anaesthesia aims for **early extubation (within about 6 hours, often 1 to 4)** after cardiac surgery, with early mobilisation and discharge from ICU, without increasing mortality or complications. Benefits are less ventilator-related lung injury and sedation, earlier mobilisation, less delirium, shorter stay and lower cost. Risks: bleeding, agitation, haemodynamic instability and reintubation.

## Patient selection

Favourable: elective, preserved ventricular function, no major comorbidity (pulmonary, renal, obesity), simple surgery (CABG, valve), short bypass time, stable haemodynamics. Unfavourable: emergency, poor ventricular function, redo or complex surgery, long bypass, bleeding, or neurological complications.

## Anaesthetic techniques

**Enhanced recovery depends on more than a short-acting anaesthetic.** Before surgery identify frailty, preoperative anaemia, sleep-disordered breathing, organ dysfunction and anticipated prolonged cross-clamp or complex intervention. During the operation avoid residual deep hypothermia, minimise transfusion where appropriate and consider fascial-plane analgesia or sternotomy-focused local techniques within anticoagulation safety constraints. In ICU, extubate only after reversible causes of impaired consciousness, significant bleeding, unstable low output, severe hypoxaemia or evolving neurological injury have been excluded. Post-extubation respiratory support, incentive breathing, effective analgesia and early physiotherapy matter as much as the extubation timestamp. The best programme audits reintubation, delirium and ICU readmission alongside ventilation time.

- **Premedication** light; avoid long-acting benzodiazepines.
- **Opioid-sparing or titrated short-acting opioids** (remifentanil, low-dose fentanyl or sufentanil), propofol or volatile agents for maintenance, rocuronium with sugammadex reversal, and **dexmedetomidine** which reduces AF and delirium.
- **Multimodal analgesia:** paracetamol, regional blocks (parasternal, erector spinae, serratus), ketamine; avoid NSAIDs in renal risk.
- Temperature control, early haemostasis and antifibrinolytic reduce bleeding.

## Extubation criteria

Normothermia, warm and haemodynamically stable with minimal vasopressors, no significant bleeding (chest drain below 100 mL/h), adequate gas exchange on low support, alert, cooperative and pain controlled, no arrhythmia, and normal acid-base and electrolytes.

## Postoperative care

Protocolised ICU or recovery care, extubation after a spontaneous breathing trial, mobilisation, early oral intake, analgesia and removal of drains and lines.

## Outcomes

Fast-track does not change mortality, but reduces ventilation hours, ICU and hospital stay; keep a low threshold for slowing the plan if bleeding, instability or unmet extubation criteria arise.

## Practical points

Agree the extubation criteria with the surgeon and ICU nurse before the patient leaves theatre, and write them in the handover. Avoid over-sedation after arrival, keep the patient warm, and treat pain early, since these are the commonest reasons that a fast-track plan fails. If bleeding or instability appears, change plan without delay and document the reason. Review the pathway periodically with audit of extubation times and reintubation rates, so that criteria can be adjusted for the local population.

**Sources:** [ERAS Cardiac/STS consensus (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.athoracsur.2023.12.006) and [BJA Education perioperative cardiac care (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.05.008) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [BJA Education perioperative AF (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.10.006)

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines fast-track and enhanced recovery
- Lists patient and surgical factors prolonging ventilation
- Lists anaesthetic and postoperative factors
- Describes anaesthetic technique for early extubation
- Gives extubation criteria
- Cautions on safety versus time targets
- Mentions routine and emergent ICU monitoring

items.title: 31. Complications of interventional cardiology procedures
items.q: Outline the major complications of interventional cardiology procedures (including percutaneous coronary intervention and transcatheter valve procedures), their presentation and their management in the catheter laboratory.
items.a:
## Why the anaesthetist is involved

Interventional procedures are increasingly done under sedation or general anaesthesia in sick patients: AF ablation, TAVI, MitraClip, left atrial appendage closure, coronary intervention for complex disease, and pacemaker or ICD implantation. The anaesthetist manages both the procedure and its complications.

## Complications

**Vascular and bleeding:** access-site haematoma, retroperitoneal bleed, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula.

**Cardiac:** **tamponade** (about 1% in AF ablation; the commonest major cause of death), coronary occlusion or dissection, arrhythmia (VF, bradyarrhythmia, heart block), valve injury, device embolisation.

**AF ablation specifics (2021 chapter):** major complications about 2%, left atrial–oesophageal fistula (about 0.1%, mortality above 90%), phrenic nerve injury (about 5% with cryoballoon), pulmonary vein stenosis, stroke and air embolism.

**Neurological:** stroke from thrombus, air or debris.

**Contrast and radiation:** contrast nephropathy, anaphylaxis, radiation exposure.

## Gas embolism

Detected by TOE (down to about 0.02 mL/kg), presenting with hypotension, arrhythmia, falling end-tidal CO2 and hypoxia. Treatment: stop the source and nitrous oxide, **FiO2 1.0**, volume and vasopressors, position according to the clinical setting and source (routine head-down/left lateral positioning has uncertain benefit), aspirate via a suitable central line if feasible, supportive care and **hyperbaric oxygen** for cerebral or large embolism.

## Anaesthetic management

**Recognise procedure-specific catastrophe rather than a generic cath-lab arrest.** After PCI, abrupt shock with ST changes may reflect coronary perforation, vessel closure, no-reflow or dissection; immediate angiographic diagnosis determines covered stent, balloon tamponade, pericardial drainage or surgical rescue. Following TAVI, profound instability may be due to annular rupture, coronary ostial obstruction, valve embolisation, severe AR or complete heart block. After left atrial ablation, tamponade is immediate, whereas atrio-oesophageal fistula can present days to weeks later with fever, neurological events or sepsis and must never be investigated by oesophageal instrumentation when suspected. A functioning airway, working defibrillator, pacing and blood-access plan are essential before the drapes or imaging equipment limit access.

- **AF ablation:** general anaesthesia preferred (immobility and airway control), often remifentanil with TIVA, jet or high-frequency low-volume ventilation, TOE to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus, **heparin** to an institution-specific ACT target, commonly ≥300 seconds, typically instituted before or immediately after transseptal access, uninterrupted anticoagulation.
- Maintain a stable rhythm and haemodynamics, with defibrillation pads and rescue pacing ready.
- Keep reversal of heparin (protamine) and surgical backup for tamponade (pericardiocentesis, thoracotomy).

Recognition of tamponade is a priority: falling pressure, rising CVP, loss of the pulse pressure and a pericardial effusion on echo.

## Practical points

Before any procedure under sedation, brief the team on how the airway will be secured if the patient becomes unstable and who will call the surgeon. Keep a clear route to the patient, as the equipment in a cath lab often obstructs access, and plan the transfer destination for complications.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, AF ablation and vascular gas embolism](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [BJA Education TAVI, Part 1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.01.004) and [Part 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534921000202)

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies coronary perforation and tamponade with management
- Lists arrhythmia and block, vessel closure and no-reflow
- Access site and retroperitoneal bleeding
- Stroke, contrast reactions and AKI
- Valve procedure complications and surgical back-up
- Anaesthetic role and preparation in a remote site

items.title: 32. Heart transplant recipient for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: A patient who received a heart transplant 3 years ago presents for non-cardiac surgery. Describe the physiology of the transplanted heart and the perioperative considerations, including drug choices.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2019, "Perioperative management of heart transplantation" (Edwards, Allen).

### Physiology of the denervated heart

- Vagal and sympathetic supply is cut. The SA node runs at its intrinsic rate of **90 to 100 beats/min**.
- The heart cannot mount a reflex tachycardia to hypovolaemia, vasodilation or afterload change; cardiac output depends on **preload** and slow rise of circulating catecholamines. It is "preload dependent".
- Angina may be absent, so **ischaemia can be silent**, although reinnervation may restore symptoms. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is suspected from new wall motion or diastolic abnormalities or ventricular arrhythmias; coronary angiography with IVUS/OCT and other modalities is selected by the transplant service; IVUS can detect early intimal disease but is not the sole diagnostic test.
- Reinnervation is partial and unpredictable (sympathetic from 6 to 8 months, parasympathetic 1 to 3 years).
- Arrhythmias: conduction delay and heart block, arrhythmia and pacing rates vary by timing, surgical technique and cohort; ventricular arrhythmias suggest rejection or CAV. Double P waves can occur. Carotid sinus massage and Valsalva have no effect.

### Drug responses

| Drug | Effect |
|---|---|
| Atropine, glycopyrrolate | Usually absent/unreliable response; variable reinnervation; use direct chronotropy/pacing |
| Ephedrine | Mixed direct/indirect; effect can be reduced or unpredictable |
| Noradrenaline, adrenaline, dobutamine | Exaggerated (more adrenoreceptors): titrate |
| Phenylephrine, metaraminol | Effective, no reflex bradycardia |
| Isoprenaline | Effective; use for bradycardia |
| Adenosine | Exaggerated bradycardia |
| Neostigmine | Bradycardia possible, especially beyond 6 months |

### Other issues

BJA Education 2021 (heart transplantation) adds that **primary graft dysfunction** is the main cause of early death, and that mechanical support (ideally ECMO) should be started early when graft dysfunction does not respond to moderate-dose inotropes.


Immunosuppression (calcineurin inhibitors: nephrotoxicity; continue on time), infection risk (asepsis, antibiotics), malignancy (more than 10% develop de novo cancer; skin cancers 100 times), tricuspid regurgitation, and drug interactions with tacrolimus or ciclosporin. Monitor ECG, arterial line for major surgery, and warm, preload-aware induction.

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains denervation, resting rate of 90 to 100 and absent reflex tachycardia
- Notes preload dependence and silent ischaemia
- Describes atropine/glycopyrrolate responses as unreliable and names direct chronotropy/pacing alternatives
- Describes exaggerated responses to catecholamines
- Mentions CAV, arrhythmias and pacemaker risk
- Covers immunosuppression and infection precautions

**Audit evidence map:** BB19; ISHLT23. Source depth and any limitations are recorded in the audit register.
